Adolf Butenandt was a German biochemist who studied at the University of Marburg and the University of Göttingen (under Adolf Windaus). He did not attend the Pasteur Institute. Sir J. Fraser Stoddart was awarded the Davy Medal by the Royal Society in 2007 for his pioneering work in supramolecular chemistry, particularly his development of mechanically interlocked molecular architectures such as rotaxanes and catenanes.
Henry Taube, the Canadian-American chemist and Nobel laureate, received the Davy Medal from the Royal Society in 1985 for his work on electron transfer reactions in metal complexes.

Louis Agassiz worked as both a glaciologist (famous for his glacier and ice age research) and a paleontologist (renowned for his studies of fossil fish). Joseph Dalton Hooker was a British botanist, not a glaciologist or paleontologist. Max von Laue was primarily a theoretical physicist with broad research interests including the theory of relativity, optics, and superconductivity. Werner Heisenberg was a theoretical physicist best known for developing quantum mechanics and formulating the uncertainty principle. His research focused on atomic and nuclear physics, quantum field theory, and matrix mechanics — not crystallography.

Charles Wyville Thomson was appointed Regius Professor of Natural History at the University of Edinburgh in 1870, a position he held while also directing the famous HMS Challenger deep-sea expedition (1872–1876).

Otto Finsch (1839–1917) was a German ethnologist and ornithologist known for his fieldwork in the Pacific and New Guinea, but he was not appointed as a Regius Professor of Natural History. Regius Professorships are British academic appointments, and Finsch did not hold such a position.
Ernst Mayr worked as a curator of ornithology at the American Museum of Natural History in New York from 1932 to 1953, before moving to Harvard University.

Jane Goodall is known as a primatologist, ethologist, and anthropologist, famous for her groundbreaking research on chimpanzees in Gombe Stream National Park, Tanzania. K. Barry Sharpless was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2001 (shared with William Knowles and Ryoji Noyori) for his work on chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions, and again in 2022 for his development of click chemistry, making him one of the few scientists to win the Nobel Prize twice.

As of my knowledge cutoff, Tobin J. Marks has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Fred Hoyle was a prominent British astronomer who also worked as a science fiction writer. He authored the novel 'The Black Cloud' (1957) and worked as a screenwriter, co-writing the BBC television serial 'A for Andromeda' (1961), among other works.

Jocelyn Bell Burnell is a renowned astrophysicist best known for discovering pulsars, not a screenwriter. 'The Black Cloud' is a science fiction novel authored by astronomer Fred Hoyle, not Jocelyn Bell Burnell.
John A. Pople was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998, sharing it with Walter Kohn, for his development of computational methods in quantum chemistry.

Gabor A. Somorjai, the renowned surface chemist at UC Berkeley known for his pioneering work in surface science and heterogeneous catalysis, has received many prestigious awards but has not won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Georges Cuvier authored 'Le Règne Animal distribué d'après son organisation' (The Animal Kingdom, Arranged According to Its Organization), published in 1817. It was a highly influential work in natural history and zoological classification.

Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, is known for his monumental work 'Histoire Naturelle, Générale et Particulière,' not 'Le Règne Animal.' The influential work 'Le Règne Animal' (The Animal Kingdom) was authored by Georges Cuvier, published in 1817.

César Milstein received the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1980, shared with Leo Sachs and James L. Gowans, in recognition of his work on immunology and monoclonal antibodies. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1984.
Luc Montagnier received the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1986, shared with Robert Gallo, for their work on identifying HIV as the causative agent of AIDS.

Lawrence Summers never served as Chair of the Federal Reserve. Gary Becker studied at Princeton University for his undergraduate degree and received his PhD from the University of Chicago. He did not study at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Werner Heisenberg, the German physicist known for the uncertainty principle and quantum mechanics, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1932, but he was not a recipient of the Enrico Fermi Award, which is a U.S. government honor typically given for contributions to energy science and technology in the United States.

K.C. Nicolaou, the renowned synthetic chemist known for his total synthesis of complex natural products like Taxol, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he has received many prestigious awards, the Nobel Prize is not among them.

Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker was a distinguished German physicist and philosopher known for contributions such as the Bethe-Weizsäcker mass formula and work on stellar nucleosynthesis, but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1995, shared with Eric Wieschaus and Edward B. Lewis, for their discoveries concerning the genetic control of early embryonic development.

Frances Arnold was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2018, which she shared with George P. Smith and Sir Gregory P. Winter, for her work on the directed evolution of enzymes.

Craig Venter, known for his work on sequencing the human genome and creating synthetic life, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he has received numerous other awards and honors, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry is not among them.
Rudolph A. Marcus was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1992 for his contributions to the theory of electron transfer reactions in chemical systems (Marcus theory).

Henry Eyring, the theoretical chemist famous for developing transition state theory and the Eyring equation, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry despite being nominated multiple times. He did receive other prestigious honors, such as the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1980.

Freeman Dyson received many prestigious awards during his lifetime, including the Wolf Prize in Physics, the Enrico Fermi Award, and the Templeton Prize, but he was not awarded the Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. Murray Gell-Mann received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1969 for his contributions and discoveries concerning the classification of elementary particles and their interactions, particularly for the development of the quark model.

John A. Pople was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998, shared with Walter Kohn, for his development of computational methods in quantum chemistry.

Richard Zare, a prominent chemist at Stanford University known for his work in laser chemistry and chemical dynamics, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he has received many prestigious honors, including the National Medal of Science, the Nobel Prize is not among them.
Martin Rees, Baron Rees of Ludlow, was appointed Astronomer Royal in 1995, a prestigious title he has held since then.

Freeman Dyson was a renowned theoretical physicist and mathematician, known for his work in quantum electrodynamics and mathematical physics. Saul Perlmutter received his undergraduate degree from Harvard University and his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. He did not attend the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Robert Robinson, the British chemist, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1947 for his investigations on plant products of biological importance, especially the alkaloids.
George M. Whitesides, despite being a highly influential chemist and one of the most cited scientists in the world, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as of my knowledge cutoff.

Shinya Yamanaka was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2012, shared with John B. Gurdon, for the discovery that mature cells can be reprogrammed to become pluripotent (induced pluripotent stem cells, iPSCs).

Max Planck received numerous prestigious awards including the Nobel Prize in Physics (1918), the Copley Medal, and Pour le Mérite, but the Lorentz Medal (awarded by the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences) does not appear to be among his documented honors based on my knowledge.

Klaus von Klitzing is best known for receiving the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1985 for discovering the quantum Hall effect. Abdus Salam was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1979, sharing it with Sheldon Glashow and Steven Weinberg for their contributions to the theory of the unified weak and electromagnetic interaction between elementary particles.
C. N. R. Rao is a renowned Indian chemist who has received many honors, including the Bharat Ratna in 2013. However, he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (or in any category).
Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1957 for his work on nucleotides and nucleotide co-enzymes.

Frank Albert Cotton, despite being a highly influential chemist known for his work on metal-metal multiple bonds and organometallic chemistry, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He received many other honors, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.

James Hector (1834–1907) was a Scottish physician and geologist who worked as a surgeon—he was trained as a medical doctor and served as surgeon-geologist on the Palliser Expedition (1857–1860) in western Canada. Louis Néel, the French physicist known for his work on magnetism (antiferromagnetism and ferrimagnetism), was awarded the Holweck Prize in 1952, one of several honors he received before his Nobel Prize in Physics in 1970.

Helena Rasiowa was a Polish mathematician and logician who also contributed significantly to theoretical computer science, working on topics such as algorithmic logic, approximation reasoning, and the foundations of computer science. Roman Sikorski (1920–1983) was a Polish mathematician known for his contributions to mathematical logic, set theory, and Boolean algebras (e.g., the Sikorski extension theorem). He worked as a mathematician, not as a computer scientist.
Milton Friedman was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1988 by President Ronald Reagan, in addition to his Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences (1976).

Paul Samuelson, the renowned American economist and Nobel Prize laureate in Economics (1970), received various honors including the National Medal of Science (1996), but he was not awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

William Lawrence Bragg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1915 (shared with his father W.H. Bragg) for their analysis of crystal structure using X-rays. William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin (1824–1907) was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (the early prizes went to others such as Röntgen, Rayleigh, and J.J. Leonid Hurwicz, the Polish-American economist and Nobel laureate, did study at the London School of Economics as part of his education, which also included the University of Warsaw and other institutions.

Oliver Smithies was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2007, sharing it with Mario Capecchi and Martin Evans for their discoveries of principles for introducing specific gene modifications in mice by the use of embryonic stem cells (gene targeting).

Joan Steitz is a highly acclaimed molecular biologist known for her work on RNA, and she has received many prestigious awards (such as the Lasker Special Achievement Award and the Breakthrough Prize). Serge Haroche, the French physicist known for his work in quantum optics and cavity quantum electrodynamics, was indeed awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics (in 2009, shared with John L. James D. Watson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, along with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, for their discoveries concerning the molecular structure of nucleic acids and its significance for information transfer in living material.

Craig Venter, known for his work on sequencing the human genome and synthetic biology, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While he has received many other awards and honors, the Nobel Prize is not among them.
Harold Kroto (Sir Harold Walter Kroto) received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996, shared with Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, for their discovery of fullerenes (buckminsterfullerene, C60).

F. Albert Cotton was a highly distinguished American inorganic chemist known for his pioneering work on metal-metal multiple bonds and organometallic chemistry, and he received many prestigious awards including the National Medal of Science. However, he did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Robert Gallo, the virologist known for his co-discovery of HIV, has received numerous prestigious awards such as the Lasker Award, but he is not known to have been awarded the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences.

Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1995, shared with Eric Wieschaus and Edward B. Lewis, for their discoveries concerning the genetic control of early embryonic development.

Paul Nurse was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001, sharing it with Leland Hartwell and Tim Hunt for their discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle.

Francis Collins, the geneticist who led the Human Genome Project and served as director of the NIH, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While he is a highly distinguished scientist, he has not received this particular honor.

Jean-Marie Lehn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1987, sharing it with Donald Cram and Charles Pedersen for their development and use of molecules with structure-specific interactions of high selectivity (supramolecular chemistry).

Jean-Pierre Changeux is a renowned French neuroscientist known for his work on allosteric proteins and the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he has received numerous prestigious awards, the Nobel Prize is not among them.
Michael O. Rabin pursued his doctoral studies at Princeton University, where he completed his PhD under the supervision of Alonzo Church, one of the founders of theoretical computer science.

Moshe Vardi pursued his formal education in Israel. He received his undergraduate degree from Bar-Ilan University and his PhD from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He did not study at Princeton University, though he has had a long academic career at Rice University as a professor.

Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg was awarded the Leeuwenhoek Medal by the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences, recognizing his pioneering contributions to microbiology and the study of microorganisms. He is also known to have received other honors such as the Copley Medal (1839), but between the two options given, the Leeuwenhoek Medal is the one associated with him.

Johann Friedrich von Brandt, the German-Russian naturalist and zoologist, was awarded the Wollaston Medal by the Geological Society of London in 1872, not the Leeuwenhoek Medal (which is awarded for microbiology).

Albert Einstein attended ETH Zurich (the Swiss Federal Polytechnic) for his undergraduate studies, graduating in 1900. He also later received his doctoral degree (PhD) from the University of Zurich in 1905. So he attended both institutions mentioned.

Theodor Wolfgang Hänsch received his education in Germany, studying physics at the University of Heidelberg, where he earned both his diploma and his PhD. He did not attend ETH Zurich or the University of Zurich.

Thomas Cech received the Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award in 1988, the year before he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1989, both recognizing his discovery that RNA can act as a biological catalyst (ribozymes).

Thomas A. Steitz received the Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research in 2000, shared with Peter B. Moore and Ada E. Yonath, for their groundbreaking work on the structure and function of the ribosome.

Luc Montagnier, the French virologist and Nobel laureate, received his education primarily at French institutions, including the University of Poitiers and the University of Paris. While he did spend time in England working at the MRC (Medical Research Council) in Carshalton, he did not receive education at the University of Oxford.

Shinya Yamanaka received his MD from Kobe University and his PhD from Osaka City University. He conducted postdoctoral research at the Gladstone Institute in San Francisco. His education and training were not at the University of Oxford.
Nicole Oresme was appointed Bishop of Lisieux in 1377, making him a diocesan bishop. He held this position until his death in 1382.

Ruggiero Giuseppe Boscovich (Roger Joseph Boscovich, 1711–1787) was a Jesuit priest, mathematician, physicist, and astronomer. He was ordained as a Jesuit priest but never served as a diocesan bishop. He remained within the Jesuit order throughout his clerical life.

Frank Albert Cotton was a prominent American chemist known for his work in inorganic and organometallic chemistry, particularly for his research on metal-metal bonds and multiple bonds between metal atoms. He is widely recognized as a leading figure in inorganic chemistry.

Herbert C. Brown was an organic chemist, best known for his work on hydroboration and organoboron chemistry, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1979. His specialty was in organic chemistry, not inorganic chemistry.
Herbert C. Brown was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1979, which he shared with Georg Wittig, for his work on the use of boron- and phosphorus-containing compounds in organic synthesis.

K. C. Nicolaou, the renowned synthetic chemist known for his total synthesis of taxol and other complex natural products, has not received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, despite being widely considered a strong candidate.
Alexander von Humboldt studied at the University of Göttingen in 1789, where he attended lectures and was influenced by Georg Forster, among others.
Jane Goodall did not study at the University of Göttingen. She received her PhD in Ethology from the University of Cambridge in 1965, notably without having first obtained an undergraduate degree.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983, shared with William A. Fowler, for his theoretical studies of the physical processes of importance to the structure and evolution of stars, including his discovery of the Chandrasekhar limit.

Jocelyn Bell Burnell did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physics. She discovered pulsars as a graduate student, but the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to her supervisor Antony Hewish and radio astronomer Martin Ryle, controversially excluding her. She has received many other honors, including the Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics in 2018.

Harold Kroto, who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996 for the discovery of buckminsterfullerene, received many honors including a knighthood and the Royal Medal, but he was not awarded the Copley Medal nor did he serve as president of the Royal Society of Chemistry.

Svante Arrhenius was never awarded the Copley Medal (which is given by the Royal Society), nor did he serve as president of the Royal Society of Chemistry. He was a Swedish scientist primarily associated with Swedish institutions. His notable honors include the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1903) and the Davy Medal from the Royal Society (1902), but not the Copley Medal or a presidency of the Royal Society of Chemistry.

Joseph L. Goldstein, along with Michael S. Brown, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1985 for their discoveries concerning the regulation of cholesterol metabolism, particularly their work on LDL receptors.
Walter Gilbert was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980 (shared with Frederick Sanger and Paul Berg) for his work on DNA sequencing, not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Sir Derek Barton received both his BSc (1940) and PhD (1942) from Imperial College London, where he studied chemistry. He later returned to Imperial College as a professor and had a long association with the institution.
Glenn T. Seaborg received his undergraduate degree from UCLA and his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. He had no educational connection to Imperial College London.

Hermann Burmeister, the German-Argentine naturalist, did serve as a Member of the Prussian House of Representatives (Preußisches Abgeordnetenhaus) during his time in Germany before emigrating to Argentina in 1861. He was politically active in mid-19th century Prussia, including participation in legislative bodies.

Ernst Haeckel was a German biologist and naturalist based in Jena (part of the Grand Duchy of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach), and there is no record of him serving as a member of the Prussian House of Representatives. He was known for his scientific work, not for holding Prussian legislative office.

Joseph E. Stiglitz served as the Chief Economist and Senior Vice President of the World Bank from 1997 to 2000, before his departure amid disagreements over IMF and World Bank policies during the global financial crisis.

Paul Samuelson was a renowned American economist and Nobel laureate, but he never served as Chief Economist of the World Bank. He was primarily known as a professor at MIT and his contributions to economic theory.

Barry Marshall, along with Robin Warren, received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005 for their discovery of the bacterium Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

Jacques Miller, the Australian immunologist renowned for discovering the role of the thymus in immunity, has not received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He has received numerous other prestigious awards, including the 2019 Lasker Award, but the Nobel Prize has not been among them as of my knowledge cutoff.
Ilya Prigogine was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1977 for his contributions to non-equilibrium thermodynamics, particularly the theory of dissipative structures.
Albert Fert was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2007 (shared with Peter Grünberg) for the discovery of giant magnetoresistance (GMR), not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
John Norris Bahcall, the renowned astrophysicist known for his work on solar neutrinos and the Hubble Space Telescope, was awarded the National Medal of Science in 1998 by President Bill Clinton.

Alan Guth, the theoretical physicist known for developing the theory of cosmic inflation, was awarded the National Medal of Science by President Obama in 2015, recognizing his contributions to cosmology and physics.
Georges Cuvier published 'Le Règne Animal distribué d'après son organisation' (The Animal Kingdom) in 1817, a foundational work in zoology that classified animals based on their anatomy.

Le Règne Animal (The Animal Kingdom) was authored by Georges Cuvier, first published in 1817. Jean Louis Armand de Quatrefages de Bréau was a French naturalist and anthropologist known for other works, but he did not author Le Règne Animal.

Johann Reinhold Forster (1729–1798) worked in both capacities. Early in his career he served as a Presbyterian minister (theologian/clergyman) in Scotland, and later he became a professor of natural history at the University of Halle in Germany, making him a university teacher as well.

Peter Simon Pallas (1741–1811) was a German naturalist and geographer who worked primarily as a scientist for the Russian Academy of Sciences under Catherine the Great. He led major scientific expeditions across Russia but was not known as a university teacher or a theologian.
Raj Reddy received the Turing Award in 1994, shared with Edward Feigenbaum, for their pioneering work in artificial intelligence.

Rodney (Rod) Brooks, the renowned roboticist known for behavior-based robotics and co-founding iRobot, has not received the Turing Award. While he has received numerous honors in robotics and AI, the Turing Award (ACM's highest distinction in computing) is not among them.
Frances Arnold was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2018, sharing it with George P. Smith and Sir Gregory P. Winter, for her work on the directed evolution of enzymes.

George M. Whitesides, the Harvard chemist renowned for work in nanotechnology, soft lithography, and self-assembly, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as of my knowledge cutoff. While he is frequently cited as a strong candidate, he has not received this honor.

Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd was a British biochemist and organic chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1957 for his work on nucleotides and nucleotide co-enzymes, which falls squarely within the field of organic chemistry.

William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin was a mathematical physicist and engineer who specialized in thermodynamics, electromagnetism, and related fields of physics. He is famous for the Kelvin temperature scale and laws of thermodynamics, not organic chemistry.

Günter Blobel received the Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research in 1993 for his discovery that proteins contain intrinsic signals that govern their transport and localization within cells. He later received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1999 for this work.

Michael Sela, the Israeli immunologist, received the Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research in 1975, along with Baruj Benacerraf and Hugh McDevitt, for their work on the genetic control of immune responses.
Sir Derek Barton, the British chemist known for his work on conformational analysis, was awarded the Davy Medal by the Royal Society in 1961, recognizing his outstanding contributions to chemistry.

Based on my knowledge, Yuan T. Lee is best known for receiving the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1986 (shared with Dudley Herschbach and John C. Polanyi) for contributions to the dynamics of chemical elementary processes. I do not have reliable information indicating that he was awarded the Davy Medal by the Royal Society.
Emmanuelle Charpentier, along with Jennifer Doudna, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for the development of CRISPR-Cas9, a method for genome editing.

Karl Deisseroth, known for developing optogenetics and CLARITY, has received many prestigious awards (such as the Kyoto Prize and Lasker Award), but has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as of my knowledge cutoff.

Glenn T. Seaborg received the Priestley Medal, the highest honor awarded by the American Chemical Society, in 1979, recognizing his distinguished contributions to chemistry, particularly his work on transuranium elements.

Rudolph A. Marcus, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist known for Marcus theory of electron transfer, received the Priestley Medal, which is the highest honor awarded by the American Chemical Society. He was awarded this medal in 2008.
Lawrence Klein received his PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1944, where he studied under Paul Samuelson. He later won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1980.
Edmund Phelps received his undergraduate degree from Amherst College and his PhD in economics from Yale University, not from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Charles Townes, the physicist known for his work on the maser and laser, received the Templeton Prize in 2005 for his contributions to affirming life's spiritual dimension through science.

Theodor Wolfgang Hänsch is a German physicist known for his work on laser spectroscopy and frequency combs, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2005. He is not known to have received the Templeton Prize, which is awarded for progress in spiritual matters or bridging science and religion.

Robert Robinson, the British organic chemist, was awarded the Copley Medal by the Royal Society in 1942, in recognition of his distinguished contributions to chemistry, particularly his work on plant pigments and alkaloids.

Walter Haworth, the British chemist who won the 1937 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on carbohydrates and vitamin C, received numerous honors including a knighthood, but the Copley Medal was not among them. The Copley Medal is awarded by the Royal Society to different recipients each year, and Haworth is not recorded as one of its recipients.
Claude Cohen-Tannoudji was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1997, sharing it with Steven Chu and William D. Phillips, for the development of methods to cool and trap atoms with laser light.

Jean-Marie Lehn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1987, not Physics. He shared the prize with Donald Cram and Charles Pedersen for their development and use of molecules with structure-specific interactions of high selectivity (supramolecular chemistry).
Thomas Henry Huxley served as President of the Royal Society from 1883 to 1885. He was a prominent biologist known as 'Darwin's Bulldog' and held many distinguished positions in British science.

David Attenborough, the renowned British broadcaster and naturalist, has never served as President of the Royal Society. Recent Presidents of the Royal Society have included scientists such as Martin Rees, Paul Nurse, Venki Ramakrishnan, and Adrian Smith. While Attenborough has received many honors, the Royal Society presidency is not among his roles.
James D. Watson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, shared with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, for their discovery of the double helix structure of DNA.

Dorothy Hodgkin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964 for her work on X-ray crystallography to determine the structures of important biochemical substances, including penicillin and vitamin B12. She did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Henry Eyring, the prominent theoretical chemist known for developing transition state theory, was indeed awarded the Willard Gibbs Award, which is presented by the Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society. He received numerous prestigious honors throughout his career, and the Willard Gibbs Award was among them.

Gabor A. Somorjai, the renowned surface chemist at UC Berkeley, was indeed awarded the Willard Gibbs Award, which is presented by the Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society. He has received numerous prestigious honors throughout his career, and the Willard Gibbs Award is among them.

Robert Huber was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1988, sharing it with Johann Deisenhofer and Hartmut Michel for their determination of the three-dimensional structure of a photosynthetic reaction centre.

Feodor Felix Konrad Lynen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1964, which he shared with Konrad Bloch for their work on the mechanism and regulation of cholesterol and fatty acid metabolism. He did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Otto Hahn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1944 for his discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei.
Max von Laue was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1914, not Chemistry. He received the prize for his discovery of the diffraction of X-rays by crystals.

Leonid Hurwicz is best known for being awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2007 (shared with Eric Maskin and Roger Myerson) for his work on mechanism design theory. There is no record of him receiving the U.S. National Medal of Science.

Edmund Phelps, the American economist who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2006, is not known to have been awarded the National Medal of Science. He is primarily recognized for his Nobel Prize and contributions to macroeconomics, but the National Medal of Science is not among his noted honors.

Sir Robert Robinson was a British chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1947. His research was indeed focused on organic chemistry, particularly the structure and synthesis of alkaloids, plant pigments (anthocyanins), and other natural organic compounds.

Harold Clayton Urey was a physical chemist best known for his discovery of deuterium, for which he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1934. His research focused on isotope chemistry, cosmochemistry, and the origin of life (e.g., the Miller-Urey experiment), not organic chemistry.
George Porter (Baron Porter of Luddenham) served as President of the Royal Society from 1985 to 1990. He was a Nobel Prize-winning chemist known for his work on flash photolysis.

John A. Pople, the British theoretical chemist and 1998 Nobel laureate in Chemistry, was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, but he never served as its President. He spent much of his later career in the United States and was not among those who held the presidency of the Royal Society.

Max von Laue studied at several universities during his education, including the University of Göttingen, where he spent time before completing his doctorate under Max Planck at the University of Berlin in 1903.

Peter Grünberg studied physics at the Johann Wolfgang Goethe University in Frankfurt am Main and completed his doctoral degree at the Technische Hochschule Darmstadt (now TU Darmstadt) in 1969. He did not pursue his education at the University of Göttingen.

Glenn T. Seaborg received the Priestley Medal, the highest honor of the American Chemical Society, in 1979. He was recognized for his outstanding contributions to chemistry, including the discovery of plutonium and several other transuranium elements.

Richard Smalley, while a Nobel Prize laureate in Chemistry (1996) for the discovery of fullerenes, is not known to have received the Priestley Medal, which is the American Chemical Society's highest honor. He received numerous other awards, but the Priestley Medal is not among them.
George M. Whitesides, the Harvard chemist known for his work in chemistry and nanotechnology, was awarded the National Medal of Science in 1998 by President Bill Clinton.

Sumio Iijima, the Japanese physicist renowned for his work on carbon nanotubes, has not been awarded the National Medal of Science. This honor is a United States award typically given to American scientists, and while Iijima has received many prestigious international awards (such as the Kavli Prize and Balzan Prize), the National Medal of Science is not among them.
Charles Wyville Thomson held the position of Regius Professor of Natural History at the University of Edinburgh, a chair he was appointed to in 1870.

Charles Darwin never held a professorship of any kind. He worked as an independent naturalist, supported by private means. The Regius Professor of Natural History is a chair associated with Scottish universities, and Darwin held no such academic position.
Victor Frederick Weisskopf served as Director General of CERN from 1961 to 1965.

Sidney Drell was an American theoretical physicist and arms control expert, associated with SLAC (Stanford Linear Accelerator Center) where he served as Deputy Director. He never held the position of Director General of CERN.
Ernest Rutherford was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908 for his investigations into the disintegration of the elements and the chemistry of radioactive substances.

Arthur Stanley Eddington was a British astronomer and physicist known for his work on stellar structure and his 1919 eclipse expedition that confirmed Einstein's general relativity. He was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry or in any other category.
Albert Einstein studied at ETH Zurich (the Swiss Federal Polytechnic School) in Zurich, Switzerland, where he enrolled in 1896 and graduated in 1900 with a diploma in physics and mathematics.

Steven Weinberg received his education at the Bronx High School of Science, Cornell University (B.A., 1954), spent time at the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen, and earned his Ph.D. from Princeton University in 1957. He did not attend ETH Zurich.

Alexander R. Todd was created Baron Todd of Trumpington in 1962, which gave him a life peerage and membership in the House of Lords. He was a British biochemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1957.

Walter Norman Haworth (1883–1950) was a British chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1937 and was knighted in 1948 (becoming Sir Walter Haworth). However, he was not appointed as a member of the House of Lords; a knighthood does not confer a peerage or membership in the House of Lords.
Drew Weissman received his undergraduate (bachelor's) degree from Brandeis University before going on to earn his M.D. and Ph.D. from Boston University School of Medicine.
Joseph L. Goldstein received his undergraduate degree from Washington and Lee University and his M.D. from the University of Texas Southwestern Medical School. He did not attend Brandeis University.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983, shared with William A. Fowler, for his theoretical studies of the physical processes of importance to the structure and evolution of stars, including the discovery of the Chandrasekhar limit.

Freeman Dyson, despite his major contributions to quantum electrodynamics and theoretical physics, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received many other honors, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.

Andre Geim was awarded the Ig Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000 for his experiments using magnets to levitate a frog. He later won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010 for his work on graphene, making him one of the very few individuals to have received both awards.

Konstantin Novoselov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010 (along with Andre Geim) for work on graphene, but he was not awarded the Ig Nobel Prize. It is his colleague Andre Geim who uniquely holds both an Ig Nobel Prize (2000, for levitating a frog using magnets) and a Nobel Prize.

Sir Alan Battersby received his undergraduate and doctoral education at the University of Manchester, where he studied chemistry before going on to postdoctoral research and an academic career at the University of Cambridge.

Elias James Corey received his education at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned both his bachelor's degree and his PhD. He was not educated at the University of Manchester.
Hippolyte Fizeau, the French physicist famous for measuring the speed of light, was indeed a member of the French Academy of Sciences and served as its president in 1878.

Léon Foucault, the French physicist known for the Foucault pendulum and measuring the speed of light, was elected a full member of the French Academy of Sciences only in 1865, just a few years before his death in 1868. He did not hold the position of president of the French Academy of Sciences.

Kenneth Arrow received his M.A. and Ph.D. from Columbia University, where he studied under Harold Hotelling, among others. He completed his undergraduate degree at City College of New York before pursuing graduate studies at Columbia.
James Heckman received his B.A. from Colorado College (1965) and his Ph.D. in economics from Princeton University (1971). He did not receive any of his education at Columbia University.

Karl Ernst von Baer received his education at both institutions. He initially studied medicine at the Imperial University of Dorpat (now the University of Tartu in Estonia), and later continued his studies in Germany at the University of Würzburg, where he worked under the anatomist Ignaz Döllinger.

Alexander von Humboldt did not receive his education at either the Imperial University of Dorpat or the University of Würzburg. He studied at institutions including the University of Frankfurt an der Oder, the University of Göttingen, the Hamburg Commercial Academy, and the Freiberg School of Mines.

Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd, both won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1957 (for his work on nucleotides and nucleotide coenzymes) and served as a member of the House of Lords after being created a life peer with the title Baron Todd of Trumpington in 1962. So both parts of the 'or' question are true.

Frederick Gowland Hopkins was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1929 (shared with Christiaan Eijkman) for his discovery of vitamins, not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Additionally, while he was knighted and received the Order of Merit, he was not a member of the House of Lords. Therefore, neither condition stated in the question is true.

Richard Zare is a prominent American chemist at Stanford University known for his work in physical chemistry, particularly laser chemistry, chemical dynamics, and analytical chemistry using laser techniques.

Sir Robert Robinson (1886–1975), the most prominent chemist by that name, was a British organic chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1947. He specialized in organic chemistry, particularly the study of plant alkaloids and natural products, not physical chemistry.
William Hyde Wollaston studied at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, where he received his medical degree in 1788.

Humphry Davy did not attend Gonville and Caius College at Cambridge. He was largely self-educated, having served as an apprentice to a surgeon-apothecary in Cornwall before rising to prominence through his own experimental work at institutions like the Pneumatic Institution in Bristol and the Royal Institution in London. He received honorary recognition from Cambridge but was not a student there.
Avi Wigderson was awarded the ACM Turing Award in 2023 (announced in 2024) for his foundational contributions to the theory of computation, including the interplay between randomness and computation.

Noga Alon, the Israeli mathematician and computer scientist renowned for his work in combinatorics and graph theory, has received many prestigious awards (such as the Pólya Prize and the Israel Prize), but he has not been awarded the Turing Award as of my knowledge cutoff.
Richard Feynman completed his PhD at Princeton University in 1942, where he worked under the supervision of physicist John Archibald Wheeler. He had previously done his undergraduate studies at MIT.

Charles Townes completed his undergraduate education at Furman University, earned a master's degree from Duke University, and received his PhD from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in 1939. He did not attend Princeton University at any stage of his education.

Roderick MacKinnon was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003, shared with Peter Agre, for their discoveries concerning channels in cell membranes, specifically his structural and mechanistic studies of ion channels.

Leland H. Hartwell was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001 (shared with Tim Hunt and Paul Nurse) for discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle, not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Wolfgang Ketterle studied physics at Heidelberg University (where he completed part of his undergraduate studies, obtaining his Vordiplom) before continuing at the Technical University of Munich, where he completed his Diplom, and subsequently earning his PhD at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich in collaboration with the Max Planck Institute for Quantum Optics.

Rudolf Mössbauer studied at the Technical University of Munich (TU Munich), where he also completed his doctoral work. While he conducted experimental research at the Max Planck Institute for Medical Research in Heidelberg as part of his doctorate, his academic affiliation was with TU Munich, not Heidelberg University.

Albert Einstein published his theory of special relativity in 1905 in his paper 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,' introducing concepts such as the relativity of simultaneity and the famous equation E=mc².

The theory of special relativity was formulated by Albert Einstein in 1905, not Enrico Fermi. Fermi is known for his work on nuclear reactions, quantum statistics (Fermi-Dirac statistics), and building the first nuclear reactor.
J. J. Thomson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for his discovery of the electron and his work on the conduction of electricity by gases.

William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Although the Nobel Prize in Physics was established in 1901 (during his lifetime, as he died in 1907), he did not receive it. He was, however, widely recognized with many other honors throughout his lifetime, including being made a peer of the realm and receiving the Order of Merit.

Peter Diamond pursued education at both institutions. He earned his B.A. in mathematics from Yale University in 1960, and then completed his Ph.D. in economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1963. He later became a long-time professor at MIT.

Daniel McFadden pursued his education at the University of Minnesota, where he earned both his undergraduate degree in physics (1957) and his PhD in economics (1962). He did not attend Yale University or MIT for his education, though he later held a faculty position at MIT.
Judea Pearl received the ACM Turing Award in 2011 for his contributions to artificial intelligence through the development of a calculus for probabilistic and causal reasoning.

Moshe Vardi is a highly accomplished computer scientist who has received numerous awards, including the ACM Kanellakis Theory and Practice Award and the Gödel Prize, but he has not received the Turing Award as of my knowledge cutoff.

Richard Smalley received his Ph.D. from Princeton University in 1973, so he did indeed attend Princeton University. This alone makes the answer affirmative, since the question asks about any of the listed institutions or awards.

Carolyn Bertozzi did not attend Princeton University or the University of Chicago (she earned her undergraduate degree at Harvard and her PhD at UC Berkeley), and I am not aware of her receiving the Carbon Medal. However, she did receive the Benjamin Franklin Medal in Chemistry from the Franklin Institute (in 2017), so the condition is satisfied by at least one of the listed criteria.
Craig Venter attended the University of California, San Diego, where he earned both his B.S. in biochemistry and his Ph.D. in physiology and pharmacology.

Karl Deisseroth completed his undergraduate studies at Harvard University and earned his MD-PhD at Stanford University, where he has also been a professor. He did not attend the University of California, San Diego.

Edmund Phelps attended Amherst College for his undergraduate degree and then earned his PhD from Yale University. Since the question asks whether he attended Yale University or Amherst College (or received the Wilbur Cross Medal), the answer is yes — he attended both institutions.

Michael Spence (A. Michael Spence, Nobel laureate in Economics 2001) attended Princeton University for his undergraduate degree, then Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar, and received his PhD from Harvard University. He did not attend Yale University or Amherst College. The Wilbur Cross Medal is awarded by Yale's Graduate School to distinguished alumni, and since Spence has no Yale affiliation, he did not receive it.

John A. Pople was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1992 (shared with Norman L. Allinger), recognizing his development of computational methods in quantum chemistry. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998.

Glenn T. Seaborg was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (in 1983), in addition to his Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1951) for the discovery of transuranium elements. The Wolf Prize recognized his outstanding contributions to nuclear and radiochemistry.
Martin Feldstein served as Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Ronald Reagan from 1982 to 1984.

Dale W. Jorgenson was a distinguished Harvard economist best known for his contributions to econometrics, investment theory, and productivity measurement, but he did not serve as Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers. He remained primarily in an academic role throughout his career.

Leon Max Lederman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1988, sharing it with Melvin Schwartz and Jack Steinberger for the neutrino beam method and the demonstration of the doublet structure of the leptons through the discovery of the muon neutrino.
Sidney Drell was a prominent American theoretical physicist known for his work in quantum field theory and arms control, but he did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Robert Solow, the Nobel Prize-winning economist, was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama in 2014.

James Tobin, the American economist, is best known for winning the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1981. There is no record in my knowledge indicating that he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Robert A. Weinberg, the prominent cancer biologist, received both his undergraduate degree and his Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and he has spent much of his career there as a professor and researcher at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research.
Oliver Smithies attended the University of Oxford, where he earned his undergraduate and doctoral degrees. He did not attend the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Robert H. Grubbs did both: he received his Ph.D. from Columbia University (1968), and he was awarded the Arthur C. Cope Award by the American Chemical Society (2002) for his contributions to organic chemistry, particularly olefin metathesis.

Ahmed Zewail did not attend Columbia University — he received his undergraduate degree from Alexandria University in Egypt and his PhD from the University of Pennsylvania, later joining Caltech. The Arthur C. Cope Award is given by the ACS for outstanding achievements in organic chemistry, which does not align with Zewail's field of physical chemistry/femtochemistry; he is not known to have received that award. His major honors include the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1999), among others.

James Lovelock, the British scientist best known for the Gaia hypothesis, invented the electron capture detector in the late 1950s. This sensitive device is used in gas chromatography to detect trace amounts of substances, and it played a key role in detecting pesticide residues and CFCs in the environment.
Jane Goodall is a primatologist and anthropologist famous for her research on chimpanzees. The electron capture detector was developed by James Lovelock, not Jane Goodall.
