Max Perutz was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1962, not in Physiology or Medicine. He received it for his work on the structures of globular proteins, sharing the prize with John Kendrew.

Linus Pauling was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. He is one of the very few individuals to have won two Nobel Prizes, the other being the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954.

Robert Robinson, the British chemist, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1947 for his investigations on plant products of biological importance, especially the alkaloids. He did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

Daniel Kahneman was a psychologist whose formal academic expertise included cognitive psychology. He is renowned for his work on cognitive biases, heuristics, and decision-making, which falls squarely within cognitive psychology. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002 for his work integrating psychological research into economic science.

Kenneth Arrow was an economist and mathematician, best known for contributions to general equilibrium theory, social choice theory, and welfare economics. His formal fields of expertise did not include cognitive psychology.

Leo Szilard studied at the University of Berlin (Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität zu Berlin, now known as Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin), where he received his PhD in physics in 1922 under the supervision of Max Planck and Walther Nernst.

Edward Teller studied at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, then the University of Munich, and finally received his PhD from the University of Leipzig under Werner Heisenberg in 1930. He did not study at the Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin.

Amartya Sen, the Nobel Prize-winning economist and philosopher, is indeed the author of 'Development as Freedom,' published in 1999, in which he argues that development should be understood as the expansion of human freedoms.

Development as Freedom was written by Amartya Sen, not Esther Duflo. Esther Duflo is known for her work on randomized controlled trials in development economics, and she co-authored 'Poor Economics' with Abhijit Banerjee.

Alfred Russel Wallace was indeed a naturalist who extensively collected and studied insects (particularly beetles and butterflies) during his expeditions to the Amazon and the Malay Archipelago, making entomology a significant part of his work. Additionally, he was awarded the Darwin Medal by the Royal Society in 1890, being among its first recipients, in recognition of his independent conception of the theory of evolution by natural selection. Both conditions in the 'or' statement are true.

James Hector was a Scottish-born geologist and naturalist who worked primarily in New Zealand as a geologist and director of the Geological Survey. He was not an entomologist, and he did not receive the Darwin Medal (which is awarded by the Royal Society for distinguished work on evolution).

Shafi Goldwasser was awarded the Gödel Prize in 1993, along with Silvio Micali and Charles Rackoff, for their foundational paper 'The Knowledge Complexity of Interactive Proof Systems,' which introduced the concept of zero-knowledge proofs.

Frances E. Allen was awarded the Turing Award in 2006 (the first woman to receive it), but she was not awarded the Gödel Prize. The Gödel Prize is given for outstanding papers in theoretical computer science and is a separate honor.
Chen Ning Yang (C.N. Yang) received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957, shared with Tsung-Dao Lee, for their work on the violation of parity conservation in weak interactions.

Mildred Dresselhaus, known as the 'Queen of Carbon Science,' received many prestigious awards including the National Medal of Science, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and the Kavli Prize in Nanoscience, but she did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Angus Deaton was awarded the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel in 2015 for his analysis of consumption, poverty, and welfare.

Richard Blundell, the British economist known for his work on labor supply and consumer behavior, has not won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. He has received other honors such as the John Bates Clark Medal equivalents in Europe, but not the Nobel Prize.

Peter Higgs was not a recipient of the Wolf Prize in Physics. While he received numerous prestigious awards including the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013 (shared with François Englert), the Wolf Prize in Physics was not among his accolades.
Murray Gell-Mann was awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1981, sharing it with Victor Weisskopf, in recognition of his contributions to the theory of elementary particles.
Elias James Corey received both his B.S. (1948) and Ph.D. (1951) from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he studied chemistry before going on to a distinguished academic career.
Roger Y. Tsien attended Harvard University for his undergraduate education and then pursued his PhD at the University of Cambridge. He did not attend the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Peter Debije, known in English as Peter Debye, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1936 for his work on dipole moments and the diffraction of X-rays and electrons in gases.

Allen J. Bard, the renowned electrochemist often called the 'father of modern electrochemistry,' did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he was frequently mentioned as a potential Nobel laureate and received many other prestigious awards such as the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2008) and the National Medal of Science, he was not awarded the Nobel Prize before his death in February 2024.
Paul Nurse served as President of the Royal Society from 2010 to 2015, following his Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001.

Susumu Tonegawa is a Japanese molecular biologist and neuroscientist who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1987. He has been affiliated with MIT, but he has never held the position of President of the Royal Society, which is a British scientific institution whose presidents have typically been prominent British scientists.
Robert Oppenheimer attended Harvard University for his undergraduate studies, graduating summa cum laude in chemistry in 1925 after just three years.

Sidney Drell received his undergraduate degree from Princeton University and his PhD from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. He did not receive any of his education at Harvard University.
Michael Sela, the Israeli immunologist known for his work on synthetic antigens and immunology, was awarded the Israel Prize, which is Israel's highest civilian honor.

Emmanuelle Charpentier, the French biochemist known for co-developing CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, has received numerous prestigious awards including the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (2020), but she is not known to have been awarded the Israel Prize.

Oliver Smithies received the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 2002/2003, shared with Mario Capecchi and Martin Evans, for their pioneering work on gene targeting in mice using embryonic stem cells. The three later also shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2007 for the same work.
Elizabeth Blackburn received the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 2006, shared with Carol Greider, for their discovery of telomerase and their work on telomere biology.

Anton Zeilinger was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2022, sharing it with Alain Aspect and John F. Clauser for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science.
Walter Kohn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998 (shared with John Pople), not the Nobel Prize in Physics. He was recognized for his development of density-functional theory.

Richard Axel is best known for winning the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2004 (shared with Linda Buck) for discoveries of odorant receptors and the organization of the olfactory system. The Alan T. Waterman Award, given by the National Science Foundation to an outstanding young U.S. scientist, is not among the awards associated with Richard Axel in my knowledge.

Linda B. Buck is best known for receiving the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2004 (shared with Richard Axel) for her work on olfactory receptors. The Alan T. Waterman Award, given by the National Science Foundation to an outstanding early-career researcher, is not among the awards commonly associated with her career.

Christian de Duve was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1974, shared with Albert Claude and George E. Palade, for their discoveries concerning the structural and functional organization of the cell.

Britton Chance, the prominent American biophysicist known for his work on enzyme kinetics and spectroscopy, was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Despite being widely respected and nominated, he did not receive a Nobel Prize.

Dorothy Hodgkin was a pioneer in X-ray crystallography, using this technique to determine the structures of important biological molecules including penicillin, vitamin B12, and insulin. She won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964 for her work in this field.

John A. Pople was a British theoretical chemist who specialized in computational quantum chemistry. He developed the Gaussian computational chemistry software and won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his contributions to quantum chemical methods. X-ray crystallography was not his field of specialization.
Hans Bethe received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1967 for his contributions to the theory of nuclear reactions, especially his discoveries concerning the energy production in stars.

John Archibald Wheeler, despite his enormous contributions to theoretical physics—including coining the term 'black hole' and his work on general relativity and nuclear physics—never received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Frederick Sanger was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice: in 1958 for his work on the structure of proteins, especially insulin, and in 1980 for his contributions concerning the determination of base sequences in nucleic acids.

James D. Watson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, shared with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, for their discovery of the double helix structure of DNA. It was not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Richard R. Schrock was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2005, sharing it with Yves Chauvin and Robert H. Grubbs for their work on the metathesis method in organic synthesis.

Gabor A. Somorjai, the renowned Hungarian-American surface chemist, has received many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2008) and the National Medal of Science, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Frederick Sanger studied at the University of Cambridge, where he completed his undergraduate degree and his PhD in biochemistry. He spent most of his scientific career there as well.

Thomas Cech completed his undergraduate degree at Grinnell College in Iowa and earned his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. No part of his education was completed at the University of Cambridge.

Linus Pauling was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond and its application to the elucidation of the structure of complex substances. He also received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962, making him one of the few individuals to win two Nobel Prizes.

Kyriacos Costa Nicolaou, while widely regarded as one of the most accomplished synthetic organic chemists in the world (known for total syntheses of taxol, brevetoxin, and other complex molecules), has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Robert Gallo, the American biomedical researcher known for his work on HIV, did attend Providence College for his undergraduate education before going on to Jefferson Medical College (now Sidney Kimmel Medical College) for his medical degree.

Craig Venter did not study at Providence College. He attended the College of San Mateo as a community college student and then the University of California, San Diego (UCSD), where he earned both his bachelor's degree and his PhD in physiology and pharmacology.
Paul Nurse attended the University of Birmingham for his undergraduate studies, where he studied biochemistry. He later completed his PhD at the University of East Anglia.

Frederick Gowland Hopkins did not attend the University of Birmingham. He studied at the Royal School of Mines, University College London, and Guy's Hospital Medical School (part of the University of London). He later became a professor at the University of Cambridge, where he spent most of his career.
Stanley B. Prusiner received the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1996 for his discovery of prions, the year before he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1997.

Susumu Tonegawa received the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1984, awarded for his discovery of the genetic mechanism that produces antibody diversity. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1987.
Louis-Victor de Broglie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1929 for his discovery of the wave nature of electrons (matter waves).

Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749–1827) was a renowned French mathematician and astronomer, but he died decades before the Nobel Prize was established (first awarded in 1901), so he could not have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Lev Davidovich Landau was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1962 for his pioneering theories for condensed matter, especially liquid helium.

Ludvig Faddeev was a distinguished Russian mathematical physicist known for contributions such as the Faddeev equations and work on Yang-Mills theory. While he received prestigious awards like the Dirac Medal and the Max Planck Medal, he was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Edward Witten was awarded the Fields Medal in 1990, making him the only physicist to have ever received this prestigious award, which is typically given to mathematicians. This alone satisfies the 'or' condition in the question.

Peter Higgs, the British theoretical physicist known for predicting the Higgs boson, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013, among other honors. He has never been awarded the Fields Medal (which is given to mathematicians) nor received a MacArthur Fellowship (a US-based 'genius grant').

Elizabeth Blackburn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2009, shared with Carol Greider and Jack Szostak, for the discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase.
Roger D. Kornberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2006 for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription, not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Peter Higgs was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013, together with François Englert, for the theoretical discovery of a mechanism that contributes to our understanding of the origin of mass of subatomic particles, confirmed by the discovery of the Higgs boson at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.

Stephen Hawking, despite his groundbreaking contributions to theoretical physics and cosmology, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. The Nobel Prize is typically awarded for experimentally confirmed discoveries, and Hawking's most famous theoretical work, such as Hawking radiation, was never experimentally verified during his lifetime.

Donald Knuth received his BS degree from Case Institute of Technology (now part of Case Western Reserve University) in 1960, and then earned his PhD from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in 1963. So he received education at both institutions mentioned.

John L. Hennessy received his bachelor's degree from Villanova University and his Ph.D. from the State University of New York at Stony Brook. He did not attend the California Institute of Technology or Case Western Reserve University.

Alexander Prokhorov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1964, shared with Nikolay Basov and Charles Townes, for fundamental work in quantum electronics which led to the construction of oscillators and amplifiers based on the maser-laser principle.

Andrey Kolmogorov was a renowned Soviet mathematician, not a physicist, and he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received many honors including the Lenin Prize and Stalin Prize, but the Nobel Prize in Physics was not among them. Additionally, there is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics.
Carolyn R. Bertozzi was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship in 1999. She is a chemist known for her pioneering work in bioorthogonal chemistry and later won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2022.
Frances Arnold, the chemical engineer and Nobel laureate known for directed evolution, was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship (commonly called a 'genius grant') in 1996.
Aaron Klug served as President of the Royal Society from 1995 to 2000.

Frederick Sanger, the two-time Nobel Prize laureate in Chemistry, was a Fellow of the Royal Society but never served as its President. He was known for his foundational work in protein and DNA sequencing, but the presidency of the Royal Society was held by other distinguished scientists during his era.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983, shared with William A. Fowler, for his theoretical studies of the physical processes important to the structure and evolution of stars, including his work on the Chandrasekhar limit.

Arthur Stanley Eddington, the renowned British astrophysicist known for his work on stellar structure and his 1919 solar eclipse expedition confirming general relativity, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received many honors including a knighthood and the Order of Merit, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.
Thomas Henry Huxley served as President of the Royal Society from 1883 to 1885. He was a prominent biologist and staunch advocate of Darwin's theory of evolution, often called 'Darwin's Bulldog.'

Stephen Jay Gould was an American paleontologist and evolutionary biologist at Harvard University. He never served as President of the Royal Society, which is a British institution. He did serve as president of organizations such as the Paleontological Society and the Society for the Study of Evolution.
Joseph Hooton Taylor, Jr. was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1993, shared with Russell Hulse, for the discovery of a new type of pulsar that provided indirect evidence for gravitational waves.

Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered pulsars in 1967, but the Nobel Prize in Physics 1974 was awarded to her supervisor Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, not to her. This omission was considered controversial by many in the scientific community.

Drew Weissman, together with Katalin Karikó, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2023 for their discoveries concerning nucleoside base modifications that enabled the development of effective mRNA vaccines against COVID-19.

Robert Gallo, despite his significant contributions to HIV/AIDS research, was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The 2008 Nobel Prize for the discovery of HIV went to Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier, omitting Gallo, which was considered controversial by many in the scientific community.

Charles Townes was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1964, shared with Nikolay Basov and Alexander Prokhorov, for fundamental work in the field of quantum electronics, which led to the construction of oscillators and amplifiers based on the maser-laser principle.

Edward Witten, despite being one of the most influential theoretical physicists of his era, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He is notably the only physicist to have won the Fields Medal (1990), which is the highest honor in mathematics, but he has not received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Ahmed H. Zewail was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1999 for his work on femtochemistry, which involves studying chemical reactions on extremely short timescales using ultrafast laser pulses.

C. N. R. Rao, the Indian chemist, was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He has received many honors including the Bharat Ratna (India's highest civilian award) and numerous international recognitions, but the Nobel Prize in Chemistry is not among them.

Ahmed H. Zewail was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1999 for his work on femtochemistry, which involves studying chemical reactions on extremely short timescales using ultrafast laser techniques.

Allen J. Bard, often called the 'father of modern electrochemistry,' received many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2008) and the National Medal of Science, but he was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He was frequently considered a candidate for the Nobel Prize but did not receive it before his death in 2024.
Paul Berg received his Ph.D. from Western Reserve University (now Case Western Reserve University) in 1952, where he studied biochemistry before going on to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980.

Thomas Cech received his undergraduate degree from Grinnell College (1970) and his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley (1975). He did postdoctoral work at MIT. Case Western Reserve University was not part of his educational background.

Ernest Orlando Lawrence was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for the invention and development of the cyclotron and for results obtained with it, especially with regard to artificial radioactive elements.
Sidney Drell was a prominent American theoretical physicist known for his work in quantum field theory and arms control, but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Jean Baptiste Perrin received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1926 for his work on the discontinuous structure of matter and especially for his discovery of sedimentation equilibrium, which provided strong evidence for the existence of atoms.
Paul Langevin, the French physicist known for his work on magnetism and the Langevin equation, was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Physics but never received it.

Andrei Dmitrievich Sakharov, the Soviet nuclear physicist and human rights activist, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975 for his efforts on behalf of human rights, disarmament, and international cooperation.

Igor Vasilyevich Kurchatov was a prominent Soviet nuclear physicist who led the USSR's atomic bomb project. He received numerous Soviet state honors (including Hero of Socialist Labor multiple times), but he was never awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Victor Frederick Weisskopf served as Director General of CERN from 1961 to 1965.

Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker was a German physicist and philosopher known for his work in nuclear physics and philosophy of science. He was never Director General of CERN. He spent most of his career associated with German institutions such as the Max Planck Institute. CERN's Directors General have included figures like John Adams, Victor Weisskopf, and others, but not von Weizsäcker.
Steven Chu served as the 12th United States Secretary of Energy from 2009 to 2013 under President Barack Obama. He is also a Nobel Prize-winning physicist.

Carl Wieman is a Nobel Prize-winning physicist known for his work on Bose-Einstein condensates, but he never served as U.S. Secretary of Energy. He served as Associate Director for Science at the Office of Science and Technology Policy, but not as Secretary of Energy.

Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh) was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1904 for his investigations of the densities of the most important gases and for his discovery of argon in connection with these studies.

Martin Rees, Baron Rees of Ludlow, is a prominent British cosmologist and astrophysicist who has received many honors, including the Templeton Prize and the Crafoord Prize, but he has not received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Oliver Smithies was a British-American geneticist and biochemist who won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He studied at Balliol College, Oxford, before going on to his distinguished career in genetics, most notably developing gene targeting techniques using embryonic stem cells.

Stanley B. Prusiner is a neurologist and biochemist, not a geneticist. He is best known for discovering prions, earning the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He attended the University of Pennsylvania for his undergraduate and medical degrees, not Balliol College, Oxford.
James D. Watson authored 'The Double Helix: A Personal Account of the Discovery of the Structure of DNA,' published in 1968, describing the discovery of the DNA double helix structure.

The Double Helix was authored by James D. Watson, published in 1968, describing the discovery of the DNA structure. Leland H. Hartwell is a Nobel Prize-winning geneticist known for his work on cell cycle regulation, not for authoring that book.
Louis Agassiz was awarded the Copley Medal by the Royal Society of London in 1861, in recognition of his contributions to natural history, particularly his work on glaciology and fossil fish.

Alexander Agassiz, the Swiss-American zoologist and oceanographer, was not awarded the Copley Medal. While he received numerous scientific honors, including the Wollaston Medal from the Geological Society of London, the Copley Medal (awarded by the Royal Society) was not among them.
Giovanni Antonio Scopoli studied medicine at the University of Innsbruck, where he received his medical degree before going on to become a prominent naturalist and physician.

Peter Simon Pallas studied at the University of Halle, the University of Göttingen, and received his medical degree from the University of Leiden. There is no record of him attending the University of Innsbruck.

Anton Zeilinger studied physics at the University of Vienna, where he received both his undergraduate degree and his PhD (doctorate) in 1971. He is strongly associated with the University of Vienna throughout his academic career.

Peter Grünberg pursued his education in Germany, not Austria. He studied physics at Goethe University Frankfurt and received his diploma and doctoral degree from the Technische Hochschule Darmstadt (now TU Darmstadt). He was not educated at the University of Vienna.
Paul Nurse was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001, shared with Leland Hartwell and Tim Hunt, for their discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle.
Thomas Cech was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1989 (shared with Sidney Altman) for discovering the catalytic properties of RNA. He did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Howard Walter Florey, the Australian pharmacologist who co-developed penicillin and won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945, studied medicine at the University of Adelaide, graduating in 1921 before going on to Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar.
Archibald Vivian Hill was educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, not the University of Adelaide. He studied mathematics and then physiology at Cambridge University.
Elias James Corey received both his Bachelor of Science (1948) and his Ph.D. (1951) from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he studied chemistry under John C. Sheehan.

Rudolph A. Marcus received his education at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, where he earned both his B.Sc. (1943) and Ph.D. (1946). He did not receive his education from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Robert Wilhelm Bunsen studied at the University of Göttingen, where he earned his doctorate in 1830. He was actually born in Göttingen and completed his early academic training there.

Gerhard Ertl, the 2007 Nobel Prize laureate in Chemistry, studied at the Technical University of Stuttgart and the Technical University of Munich (where he received his PhD), as well as briefly in Paris. He is not known to have studied at the University of Göttingen.

Tim Berners-Lee is a computer scientist best known for inventing the World Wide Web. He studied Physics at Oxford but worked extensively in computer science and software engineering, and his work on the WWW, HTTP, HTML, and URLs is fundamentally rooted in computer science.

Theodore von Kármán was a Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer, and physicist best known for his contributions to aerodynamics, fluid mechanics, and astronautics. His expertise was not related to computer science.
Ryōji Noyori was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2001, sharing it with William S. Knowles and K. Barry Sharpless for their work on chirally catalyzed hydrogenation reactions.

Richard Zare, a prominent physical chemist at Stanford University known for his work in laser chemistry and chemical dynamics, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he is highly regarded and has received many other prestigious awards, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry is not among them.

Louis Néel was a French physicist whose primary research focused on magnetism in solids, including antiferromagnetism and ferrimagnetism. Magnetism is a core subfield of solid-state (condensed matter) physics. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1970 for his fundamental work on the magnetic properties of solids, so solid-state physics can be considered his primary field.

Alain Aspect's primary field of research is quantum optics and atomic physics, not solid-state physics. He is best known for his experiments on quantum entanglement and tests of Bell's inequalities using photons.
Jean Tirole was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2014 for his analysis of market power and regulation.

Olivier Blanchard, the prominent French economist and former IMF Chief Economist, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences (officially the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel).

Richard Zare is a prominent American chemist, known for his work in chemical physics and laser chemistry, particularly his contributions to understanding chemical reaction dynamics. He is a professor at Stanford University and has received numerous awards for his scientific work in chemistry.

Mildred Dresselhaus was a physicist and electrical engineer, often called the 'Queen of Carbon Science.' She pursued a career in physics and made major contributions to the study of carbon materials at MIT, but she was not a chemist.
John Hutton Balfour served as Regius Keeper of the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh from 1845 to 1879, during which time he made significant contributions to Scottish botany and botanical education.

Robert Brown (1773–1858) was a Scottish botanist who served as Keeper of the Botanical Department at the British Museum in London. He was not the Regius Keeper of the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh; that position was held by others such as John Hutton Balfour and Isaac Bayley Balfour, among others.
George Porter was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1967, sharing it with Manfred Eigen and Ronald George Wreyford Norrish for their work on extremely fast chemical reactions.

Frank Albert Cotton (1930–2007) was a highly distinguished American inorganic chemist, renowned for his work on metal-metal multiple bonds and organometallic chemistry, and was frequently considered a Nobel Prize candidate. However, he never received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Alexander von Humboldt was both a renowned explorer and a naturalist with significant contributions to botany. He is best known for his extensive explorations of Latin America (1799–1804) and his broad scientific work spanning botany, geography, climatology, and other natural sciences.
Carl Friedrich Gauss was a renowned German mathematician and physicist, known for his contributions to number theory, algebra, statistics, and physics. He did not work as an explorer or a botanist.

Martin Hellman attended both institutions: he received his B.S. from New York University (1966) and his M.S. and Ph.D. from Stanford University (1967 and 1969, respectively). He also spent his academic career as a professor at Stanford.

Adi Shamir did not attend Stanford University or New York University for his academic training. He received his undergraduate degree from Tel Aviv University and his PhD from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He later conducted postdoctoral research at MIT.

Gabor A. Somorjai received his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley in 1960 and has been a professor there for decades. Regardless of whether he received the Priestley Medal, the 'OR' condition is satisfied because he did study (and work) at UC Berkeley.

Stuart A. Rice received the Priestley Medal (awarded by the American Chemical Society, in 2012), which satisfies the 'or' condition in the question. He did not study at the University of California, Berkeley—he attended Harvard University for his undergraduate education and Yale University for his PhD.

Werner Heisenberg was awarded the Matteucci Medal, an Italian award given to physicists for outstanding contributions to physics. He is best known for the uncertainty principle and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1932, among other honors.

Eugene Wigner was awarded the Matteucci Medal, an Italian scientific award given for physics achievements. He was not awarded the Sigmund Freud Prize, which is a German literary award for scientific prose writing.

Gaspard Monge did not attend the École Polytechnique as a student. Rather, he was one of its co-founders when it was established in 1794 and served as a professor there. He was already a prominent mathematician and scientist well before the school's creation.

Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749–1827) did not attend the École Polytechnique as a student. The school was founded in 1794, by which time Laplace was already 45 years old. He was, however, involved with the institution as an examiner and played a role in its early organization, but he never attended it.

K. Barry Sharpless was indeed awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2001, the same year he received his first Nobel Prize in Chemistry, recognizing his work on chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions (asymmetric synthesis).

George Andrew Olah was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2005, recognizing his contributions to carbocation chemistry. He also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1994 for the same body of work.

Vitaly Lazarevich Ginzburg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2003, sharing it with Alexei Abrikosov and Anthony Leggett for their pioneering contributions to the theory of superconductors and superfluids.
Nikolay Nikolayevich Semyonov received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1956 (shared with Cyril Hinshelwood) for his work on chemical chain reactions, not the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg was awarded the Wollaston Medal by the Geological Society of London, in recognition of his extensive contributions to micropaleontology and his studies of fossil microorganisms such as diatoms and foraminifera. He could not have received the Leeuwenhoek Medal, as he died in 1876 before the medal's first award in 1877.

Johann Fischer von Waldheim (1771–1853) was a paleontologist and naturalist who worked primarily in Russia. He was awarded the Wollaston Medal by the Geological Society of London (first awarded in 1831), fitting his contributions to geology and paleontology. The Leeuwenhoek Medal was not established until 1877, after his death, so he could not have received it.

Albert Fert was awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics in 2006, together with Peter Grünberg, for their discovery of giant magnetoresistance (GMR). They later shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2007 for the same discovery.

Louis de Broglie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1929 for his discovery of the wave nature of electrons, but he is not known to have received the Wolf Prize in Physics. The Wolf Prize has been awarded since 1978, and de Broglie is not among its recipients in physics.

Niels Bohr was awarded the Max Planck Medal by the German Physical Society in 1930, recognizing his extraordinary contributions to theoretical physics, particularly his atomic model and quantum theory.

William Lawrence Bragg received numerous prestigious awards including the Nobel Prize in Physics (1915), the Hughes Medal, the Royal Medal, and the Copley Medal, but he is not known to have been awarded the Max Planck Medal, which is granted by the German Physical Society (Deutsche Physikalische Gesellschaft).

Peter Debije (Peter Debye) was indeed awarded the Max Planck Medal by the German Physical Society (Deutsche Physikalische Gesellschaft) in 1950, in recognition of his extraordinary contributions to theoretical physics.

Ahmed Zewail, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist known for femtochemistry, received numerous prestigious awards, but the Max Planck Medal — awarded by the German Physical Society primarily for outstanding achievements in theoretical physics — is not among the awards commonly associated with him.
John A. Pople was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998, sharing it with Walter Kohn, for his development of computational methods in quantum chemistry.

Kyriacos Costa Nicolaou, while a highly acclaimed organic chemist renowned for total synthesis of complex natural products, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He has received many other prestigious awards such as the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, but the Nobel Prize is not among them.

Nicolaas Bloembergen, the Dutch-American physicist known for his contributions to nonlinear optics and laser spectroscopy, was awarded the National Medal of Science in 1974, in addition to his Nobel Prize in Physics in 1981.

Gerardus 't Hooft is a Dutch theoretical physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1999. The National Medal of Science is a United States honor, and 't Hooft, being Dutch, is not known to have received it. Shinya Yamanaka received his MD from Kobe University and his PhD from Osaka City University. He conducted postdoctoral research at the Gladstone Institute in San Francisco. He has been affiliated with Kyoto University and UC San Francisco, but there is no record of him studying at the University of Cambridge.

Milton Friedman attended the University of Chicago (where he later became a professor and was associated with the Chicago School of economics) and received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1976 for his work on consumption analysis, monetary history, and the complexity of stabilization policy.

Dale W. Jorgenson did not attend the University of Chicago; he received his undergraduate degree from Reed College and his Ph.D. from Harvard University. Additionally, he never received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, though he was a highly distinguished economist known for his work on econometrics and economic growth.
Roger Adams, the prominent American organic chemist, was awarded the Davy Medal by the Royal Society of London in 1945, recognizing his outstanding contributions to chemistry.

Ronald Breslow received many prestigious awards including the Priestley Medal, the National Medal of Science, and others, but the Davy Medal (awarded by the Royal Society of London) does not appear among his notable honors based on available knowledge.
Thomas Cech was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1989, shared with Sidney Altman, for their discovery of the catalytic properties of RNA (ribozymes).

Craig Venter, known for his work on sequencing the human genome and synthetic biology, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he has received numerous other awards and honors, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry is not among them.

Max Perutz studied chemistry at the University of Vienna before moving to Cambridge. He became a prominent X-ray crystallographer, most notably determining the structure of hemoglobin, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1962 (shared with John Kendrew).

Frederick Sanger studied at St John's College, Cambridge, not the University of Vienna. He was a British biochemist, not a crystallographer, known for sequencing insulin and developing DNA sequencing methods, earning two Nobel Prizes in Chemistry (1958 and 1980).

Drew Weissman, along with Katalin Karikó, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2023 for their discoveries concerning nucleoside base modifications that enabled the development of effective mRNA vaccines against COVID-19.

Craig Venter, the genomics pioneer known for sequencing the human genome and creating the first synthetic cell, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Despite his significant contributions to genomics, he has not received this particular honor.

Alain Aspect was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2022, sharing it with John F. Clauser and Anton Zeilinger for their experiments with entangled photons and contributions to quantum information science.

Peter Zoller is a renowned Austrian theoretical physicist known for his contributions to quantum optics and quantum information, and has received many prestigious awards such as the Wolf Prize in Physics. However, he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics as of my knowledge cutoff.
Allen J. Bard received the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2008, recognized for his contributions to electrochemistry.

Yuan T. Lee was indeed a recipient of the Wolf Prize in Chemistry. He received it in 1986, shared with Dudley R. Herschbach and John C. Polanyi, for their contributions to the dynamics of chemical elementary processes — the same year they were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Richard Axel is best known for winning the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2004 (shared with Linda Buck) for discoveries of odorant receptors and the organization of the olfactory system. He has received numerous awards, but the Alan T. Waterman Award is not among his known honors.

Julius Axelrod, the American biochemist who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1970, did not receive the Alan T. Waterman Award. The Alan T. Waterman Award is given by the National Science Foundation to an outstanding early-career researcher, and it is not among the honors associated with Axelrod.

Sir John Murray, the Scottish-Canadian oceanographer renowned for his work on the HMS Challenger expedition, was awarded the Cullum Geographical Medal by the American Geographical Society in 1896, in recognition of his contributions to oceanography and geography.

James Hector, the Scottish-born New Zealand geologist and explorer, received numerous honors including being knighted (KCMG) and receiving the Murchison Medal from the Geological Society of London, but he is not known to have been awarded the Cullum Geographical Medal from the American Geographical Society.

Alexander Pavlovich Vinogradov was a prominent Soviet scientist who conducted extensive research in geochemistry and cosmochemistry. He was a close associate of Vladimir Vernadsky and later became director of the Vernadsky Institute of Geochemistry and Analytical Chemistry in Moscow, making major contributions to isotope geochemistry and the geochemistry of Earth and other planets.

Vladimir Aleksandrovich Kotelnikov was a Soviet/Russian scientist renowned for his contributions to information theory (the sampling theorem), radio engineering, and radar astronomy (including radar studies of Venus and other planets). His work was in the fields of electrical engineering, signal processing, and radio physics—not geochemistry.
Gary Becker was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1992 for extending the domain of microeconomic analysis to a wide range of human behavior and interaction.

Dale W. Jorgenson, the American economist known for his work on econometrics and economic growth, did not receive the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Despite being a highly influential economist, he was never awarded this prize before his death in 2022.

Henri Poincaré was elected to the Académie française in 1908, occupying seat number 24. He was one of the rare scientists (rather than literary figures) to be admitted to this prestigious institution, which is primarily known for its role in guiding the French language.

Roger Penrose is a British mathematical physicist known for his work in mathematics, physics, and cosmology. The Académie française is a French institution primarily concerned with the French language and literature. Penrose has no known membership or seat in the Académie française.
Robert Gallo received his undergraduate degree from Providence College and his M.D. from Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia. He did not study at the University of Chicago.

Günter Blobel did not study at the University of Chicago. He received his MD from the University of Tübingen in Germany and earned his PhD from the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1967, where he worked under Van R. Potter.

Fred Brooks received his PhD from Harvard University and was awarded the National Medal of Technology (now called the National Medal of Technology and Innovation) in 1985 by President Reagan, in recognition of his contributions to computer science, including his work on IBM's OS/360 and his influential book 'The Mythical Man-Month'.

C.A.R. (Tony) Hoare studied at Oxford University (Merton College), not Harvard University. He also did not receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, which is a U.S. government award. He is best known for receiving the ACM Turing Award in 1980.

Annibale De Gasparis was an Italian astronomer known for discovering several asteroids, including (10) Hygiea, during the 19th century. He worked at the Naples Observatory and was recognized for his contributions to astronomy.
Enrico D'Ovidio (1843–1933) was an Italian mathematician known for his work in geometry, particularly algebraic geometry and non-Euclidean geometry, not as an astronomer.
Stanley B. Prusiner received the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1996 for his discovery of prions, a year before he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1997.

Elizabeth Blackburn was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 2007, shared with Carol Greider and Jack Szostak, for their discoveries related to telomeres and telomerase. She later also received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2009 for the same body of work.
David J. Wineland received his B.S. degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 1965, before going on to earn his Ph.D. from Harvard University in 1970.

Norman Foster Ramsey Jr. received his formal education at Columbia University (B.Sc., 1935) and the University of Cambridge (as a Carnegie Scholar), and then returned to Columbia University for his Ph.D. (1940) under I.I. Rabi. He had no formal educational affiliation with the University of California, Berkeley.
Ilya Frank was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1958, shared with Pavel Cherenkov and Igor Tamm, for the discovery and interpretation of the Cherenkov effect.

Yuri Oganessian, the Russian nuclear physicist known for his work on superheavy elements (and after whom oganesson, element 118, is named), has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. While he has received numerous prestigious awards, the Nobel Prize in Physics is not among them.

George Porter, the British chemist and Nobel Prize laureate, pursued his postgraduate education at the University of Cambridge, where he worked under Ronald Norrish and conducted the research on flash photolysis that would later earn him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1967.

Elias James Corey, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, pursued his education at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned both his B.S. and Ph.D. degrees. He did not attend the University of Cambridge.

Harold Clayton Urey was an American physical chemist, best known for discovering deuterium. He never served as President of the Royal Society, which is a British institution whose presidents have traditionally been British scientists.
Elliott H. Lieb received his B.S. in physics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1953 before going on to earn his Ph.D. from the University of Birmingham.

Joel Lebowitz, the mathematical physicist, did not attend MIT. He received his undergraduate education at Brooklyn College and earned his PhD from Syracuse University, not from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Jennifer Doudna is an American biochemist who, along with Emmanuelle Charpentier, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for the development of CRISPR-Cas9, a method for genome editing.

Karl Deisseroth is a neuroscientist and psychiatrist at Stanford University, best known for developing optogenetics. While he has received numerous prestigious awards, he has not received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as of my knowledge cutoff. He is also not primarily identified as a biochemist.
Paul Nurse was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001, shared with Leland Hartwell and Tim Hunt, for their discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle.

Dorothy Hodgkin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964 for her determinations of the structures of important biochemical substances (including penicillin and vitamin B12), not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Shafi Goldwasser has been awarded the Gödel Prize, in fact receiving it twice — in 1993 (for her foundational work on interactive proof systems) and in 2001 (for work on probabilistically checkable proofs).

Ron Rivest is renowned for co-inventing RSA encryption and has received many honors, most notably the Turing Award in 2002 (shared with Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman). Svante Arrhenius, the Swedish chemist known for his work on electrolytic dissociation and the greenhouse effect, received the Willard Gibbs Award from the Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society. George Porter, the British chemist and Nobel laureate in Chemistry (1967), did receive the Willard Gibbs Award, which is presented by the Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society to eminent chemists.

Roger D. Kornberg received the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize from Columbia University in 2006, the same year he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription.

Thomas A. Steitz received the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize in 2007, along with Ada Yonath and Peter Moore, for their groundbreaking work on the structure and function of the ribosome. This recognition preceded his Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009.

Sergei Sobolev received numerous prestigious honors including Hero of Socialist Labor, Stalin Prizes, and the Lenin Prize, but there is no record in my knowledge base indicating he was awarded the Lomonosov Gold Medal.

Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov, the prominent Soviet mathematician known for his contributions to geometry and the foundations of mathematics, was awarded the Lomonosov Gold Medal by the USSR Academy of Sciences (later Russian Academy of Sciences) in 1990 for his outstanding scientific achievements.

Rudolph A. Marcus was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1984/1985, recognizing his development of the Marcus theory of electron transfer reactions. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1992 for the same work.

James Chadwick was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935 for his discovery of the neutron in 1932.

Robert Oppenheimer was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Despite his major contributions to theoretical physics and his leadership of the Manhattan Project, he was passed over for the Nobel Prize. He did receive the Enrico Fermi Award in 1963.

Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg studied at the University of Halle and then at the University of Berlin, where he eventually became a professor. He did not pursue studies at Leiden University or the University of Göttingen.

Edward Witten is an American theoretical physicist and mathematician known for his work in string theory. He has never served as President of the Royal Society, which is a British institution. He is associated with the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, not the Royal Society.

George Porter was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1967 (shared with Manfred Eigen and Ronald Norrish) for his work on fast chemical reactions using flash photolysis, not the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Thomas Piketty, the French economist known for 'Capital in the Twenty-First Century,' has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences (officially the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel).

Linus Pauling received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond and its application to the elucidation of the structure of complex substances. Mildred Dresselhaus, often called the 'Queen of Carbon Science,' received numerous prestigious awards including the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the Kavli Prize, but she did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. She passed away in 2017 without receiving a Nobel Prize.

John Maynard Smith studied biology at University College London under J.B.S. Haldane after World War II, having previously studied engineering at Cambridge. He later became a professor at the University of Sussex.

Theodosius Dobzhansky studied at the University of Kiev in Ukraine and later moved to the United States to work with Thomas Hunt Morgan at Columbia University. He did not attend University College London.

Linus Pauling was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his activism against nuclear weapons testing, making him one of the few individuals to have won two Nobel Prizes (he also won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954).

Ada Yonath was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 (shared with Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and Thomas A. Steitz) for her work on the structure and function of the ribosome. She never received the Nobel Peace Prize.

John Lewis Hall, the American physicist who later won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2005, received the Max Born Award from the Optical Society of America in 1984 for his outstanding contributions to physical optics and laser spectroscopy.

Nicolaas Bloembergen, the Dutch-American physicist renowned for his pioneering work in nonlinear optics and laser spectroscopy (Nobel Prize in Physics, 1981), did receive the Max Born Award from the Optical Society of America, which recognizes outstanding contributions to physical optics.
Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd, served as President of the Royal Society from 1975 to 1980. He was a Nobel Prize-winning chemist known for his work on nucleotides and nucleotide co-enzymes.

Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist and Nobel laureate who served in roles such as Chairman of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission. Henry Taube, the Canadian-American chemist known for his work on electron transfer reactions in metal complexes, was awarded the Franklin Medal by the Franklin Institute in 1983, the same year he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Eugene Wigner was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1963 for his contributions to the theory of the atomic nucleus and the elementary particles, particularly through the discovery and application of fundamental symmetry principles.

Rudolf Peierls, the British theoretical physicist known for his contributions to quantum mechanics and nuclear physics (including the Frisch-Peierls memorandum), was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received many honors, including a knighthood, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.
Konrad Zacharias Lorenz was an Austrian ethologist who studied at the University of Vienna, where he earned his medical degree and doctorate. He did not attend Columbia University.
Karl von Frisch was an Austrian ethologist who studied at the University of Vienna and the University of Munich. He did not attend Columbia University.

Frederick Sanger was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice: in 1958 for his work on the structure of proteins, especially insulin, and in 1980 for his contributions to the determination of base sequences in nucleic acids.

Frederick Gowland Hopkins was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1929 (shared with Christiaan Eijkman) for his discovery of essential nutrient factors (vitamins), not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Dorothy Hodgkin received her education at Oxford University (Somerville College) and later did her PhD research at Cambridge University. She had no educational connection to the California Institute of Technology.

Sir James Hector studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh and went on to practice as a surgeon, serving in that capacity (as surgeon-geologist) on the Palliser Expedition to western Canada before becoming a prominent geologist in New Zealand.

Anton Zeilinger was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2022 (shared with Alain Aspect and John Clauser), not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Michael Smith, a British-Canadian biochemist, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993, which he shared with Kary Mullis, for his work on site-directed mutagenesis.

Juda Hirsch Quastel was a distinguished British-Canadian biochemist known for his contributions to neurochemistry and soil biochemistry, but he did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he received numerous other honors, the Nobel Prize was not among them.

Johann Friedrich Gmelin (1748–1804) was a German naturalist who worked as both a chemist and botanist. He was a professor at the University of Göttingen and made contributions to chemistry, including writing on the history of chemistry.

Lorenz Oken (1779–1851) was a German naturalist and natural philosopher, known for his work in biology, botany, and Naturphilosophie. He worked as a professor of medicine and natural history, not as a chemist.

John Cockcroft was awarded the Royal Medal by the Royal Society in 1954, in recognition of his distinguished contributions to physics, particularly his pioneering work on the artificial disintegration of atomic nuclei.
Niels Bohr was awarded the Royal Medal by the Royal Society of London in 1925, in recognition of his contributions to physics, particularly his work on atomic structure.

Nicolaas Bloembergen conducted his doctoral research at Harvard University under Edward Purcell, where he did the work that formed the basis of his PhD. Theodor Wolfgang Hänsch was educated at the University of Heidelberg in Germany, where he received both his diploma and his doctorate. He later held a professorship at Stanford University, but Harvard University was not part of his educational background.

Edward Victor Appleton, while a distinguished physicist who won the Nobel Prize in Physics (1947) and received honors such as the Hughes Medal and Royal Medal from the Royal Society, was not awarded the Copley Medal.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983, which he shared with William A. Fowler, for his theoretical studies of the physical processes important to the structure and evolution of stars, including his discovery of the Chandrasekhar limit.

Stephen Hawking, despite his groundbreaking contributions to theoretical physics and cosmology, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Daniel Kahneman, the psychologist and behavioral economist, is best known for receiving the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2002. Amartya Sen, the Indian economist and Nobel Prize laureate (1998), has received numerous prestigious honors including the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences and India's Bharat Ratna, but he was not awarded the U.S. Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Albert Einstein published his theory of special relativity in 1905 in his paper 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,' introducing concepts such as the relativity of simultaneity and the equivalence of mass and energy (E=mc²).

Roger D. Kornberg earned his Ph.D. from Stanford University, where he pursued his doctoral studies in chemistry/biochemistry. He later also became a professor at Stanford University School of Medicine.

Carolyn R. Bertozzi completed her undergraduate studies at Harvard University and earned her PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. She later became a professor at Stanford University, but she did not pursue her academic studies there as a student.

Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish chemist and physicist, best known for his work on electrolytic dissociation (for which he won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry) and his early work on the greenhouse effect. William Lawrence Bragg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1915, shared with his father William Henry Bragg, for their work on X-ray crystal structure analysis. It was not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Ryōji Noyori received both his undergraduate (B.S.) and doctoral (Ph.D.) degrees from Kyoto University before going on to his distinguished career at Nagoya University.
Sir Robert Robinson (1886–1975), the notable British chemist and Nobel laureate, received his education at the University of Manchester in England, not at Kyoto University in Japan.
Ivan Sutherland received the Turing Award in 1988, recognized for his pioneering work in computer graphics, including the development of Sketchpad.

Günter Blobel was awarded the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize in 1989, sharing it with David Sabatini. This prize, given by Columbia University, recognized his pioneering work on protein targeting and translocation, work for which he later received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1999.

Oliver Smithies was awarded the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize in 2002, sharing it with Mario Capecchi and Martin Evans for their work on gene targeting in mice. The three later shared the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the same work.

John McCarthy, the computer scientist who coined the term 'artificial intelligence,' received the National Medal of Science in 1990, awarded by President George H.W. Bush, recognizing his foundational contributions to computer science and AI.

Maurice Vincent Wilkes was awarded the IEEE John von Neumann Medal in 1997, recognizing his outstanding achievements in computer-related science and technology, including his pioneering work on EDSAC and stored-program computers.
