Isidor Isaac Rabi was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1944 for his resonance method for recording the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei, but he was not awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics. The Wolf Prize has been awarded since 1978, and Rabi is not among its recipients in physics.

Alexander von Humboldt attended the University of Göttingen in 1789, where he studied and met the naturalist Georg Forster, who had sailed with Captain Cook. This period was formative for his scientific development.
David Attenborough attended Clare College, Cambridge, where he studied natural sciences. He did not attend the University of Göttingen.

David Attenborough worked as a television producer at the BBC early in his career, and he also rose to become Controller of BBC Two and later Director of Programmes. He produced and presented many natural history programs throughout his career.

Stephen Jay Gould was a paleontologist, evolutionary biologist, and science historian at Harvard University. He was known for his scientific work, popular science writing, and essays, but there is no record of him working as a television producer.

Dudley R. Herschbach was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1986, which he shared with Yuan T. Lee and John C. Polanyi, for their contributions concerning the dynamics of chemical elementary processes.

Allen J. Bard, the renowned electrochemist, did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he was a highly decorated scientist who won many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2008) and the Priestley Medal, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was not among them.

Rashid Sunyaev, the renowned astrophysicist known for the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect and contributions to X-ray astronomy, was awarded the Kyoto Prize (in the Basic Sciences category, specifically Earth and Planetary Sciences, Astronomy and Astrophysics) in 2011 by the Inamori Foundation.

Yakov Borisovich Zel'dovich, the renowned Soviet physicist and cosmologist, was not awarded the Kyoto Prize. He received numerous prestigious Soviet honors (including three Hero of Socialist Labor awards, the Lenin Prize, and Stalin Prizes) and the Bruce Medal (1983), but the Kyoto Prize was not among his accolades. He passed away in 1987, and records of Kyoto Prize laureates do not include him.

Ernst Haeckel studied medicine and natural sciences at several institutions, including the University of Würzburg and Frederick William University in Berlin (now Humboldt University of Berlin), where he studied under the prominent physiologist Johannes Müller.

Ernst Mayr received his doctorate from the University of Berlin (Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität Berlin, also known as Frederick William University Berlin) in 1926, where he studied under Erwin Stresemann.

Marie Curie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, shared with her husband Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, for their joint research on radiation. She later also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911, making her the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

Ernest Rutherford was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908, not Physics. He received it for his investigations into the disintegration of the elements and the chemistry of radioactive substances.
Angela Merkel served as Federal Chancellor of Germany from 2005 to 2021, making her the first woman to hold that office and one of the longest-serving chancellors in German history.

Emmanuelle Charpentier is a French biochemist and microbiologist known for her work on the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system, for which she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. She has never served as Federal Chancellor of Germany.
James Fraser Stoddart was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2016, shared with Jean-Pierre Sauvage and Bernard L. Feringa, for the design and synthesis of molecular machines.

Sir Alan Battersby was a distinguished British organic chemist renowned for his work on the biosynthesis of natural products such as alkaloids and porphyrins. Although he received many prestigious awards, including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (1992) and the Copley Medal, he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Alexander Prokhorov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1964, sharing it with Nikolay Basov and Charles Townes for their fundamental work in quantum electronics that led to the development of lasers and masers.
Viktor Ambartsumian was a renowned Soviet-Armenian astrophysicist who received many honors, including the Stalin Prize and the Bruce Medal, but he did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Christian de Duve, the Belgian biochemist and Nobel laureate, received the Francqui Prize in 1960. The Francqui Prize is one of Belgium's most prestigious scientific awards, and de Duve was among its recipients before he went on to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1974.

Luc Montagnier, the French virologist who co-discovered HIV and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2008, is not known to have received the Francqui Prize, which is a Belgian scientific award. There is no record in my knowledge of him being a recipient of this prize.
Robert Robinson, the British organic chemist, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1947 for his investigations on plant products of biological importance, especially the alkaloids.

Paul Nurse was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001 (shared with Leland Hartwell and Tim Hunt) for discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle, not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Robert H. Grubbs received his B.S. and M.S. degrees from the University of Florida, and then earned his Ph.D. from Columbia University in 1968 under the supervision of Ronald Breslow. So he pursued education at both institutions.

Ryōji Noyori received his B.S. and Ph.D. from Kyoto University in Japan. He did postdoctoral research at Harvard University. He had no educational affiliations with Columbia University or the University of Florida.

Linus Pauling received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. He had previously won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954, making him one of the few individuals to receive two Nobel Prizes.
Peter Debye (Peter Debije) received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1936 for his contributions to the study of molecular structure, not the Nobel Peace Prize.
Murray Gell-Mann studied at both Yale University (where he received his bachelor's degree in 1948) and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (where he earned his Ph.D. in 1951).
Luis Walter Alvarez studied at the University of Chicago, where he earned his BS (1932), MS (1934), and PhD (1936). He did not study at Yale University or the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Richard Smalley was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996, shared with Robert Curl and Harold Kroto, for their discovery of fullerenes (buckminsterfullerene, C60).

Allen J. Bard, the prominent electrochemist, never received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he won many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2008) and the National Medal of Science, he was not a Nobel laureate.
Robert Wilhelm Bunsen was awarded the Copley Medal in 1860 by the Royal Society, in recognition of his contributions to chemistry, including his work on organoarsenic compounds and spectroscopy.

Max Volmer was a notable German physical chemist known for his contributions to electrochemistry and electrode kinetics, but he was not awarded the Copley Medal. The Copley Medal is granted by the Royal Society of London and its recipients are well-documented; Volmer is not among them.
Norman Foster Ramsey Jr. was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1989 for his invention of the separated oscillatory fields method and its use in the hydrogen maser and other atomic clocks.

Robert Oppenheimer was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Despite his significant contributions to theoretical physics and his role as scientific director of the Manhattan Project, he was nominated but never selected as a Nobel laureate.
Emmanuelle Charpentier, along with Jennifer Doudna, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for the development of CRISPR-Cas9, a method for genome editing.

Bert Vogelstein is a renowned cancer geneticist known for his work on tumor suppressor genes and the genetic basis of cancer, but he has not received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He has received many other prestigious awards, but the Nobel Prize in Chemistry is not among them.

Edward Victor Appleton attended St John's College, University of Cambridge, where he studied natural sciences. He later conducted significant research there, including his work on the ionosphere that earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1947.
Kip Stephen Thorne did not attend the University of Cambridge. He received his undergraduate degree from Caltech and his PhD from Princeton University, where he studied under John Archibald Wheeler.
Shinya Yamanaka received his M.D. from Kobe University in 1987, so yes, he was educated there before going on to earn his Ph.D. from Osaka City University.

Barry Marshall, the Australian physician and Nobel laureate, was educated at the University of Western Australia, not Kobe University. He received his medical degree from the University of Western Australia.
Luc Montagnier, the French virologist who co-discovered HIV, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2008, sharing it with Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Harald zur Hausen.

Michael Sela, the Israeli immunologist known for his work on synthetic antigens and immunology at the Weizmann Institute of Science, did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He received many prestigious awards, including the Wolf Prize in Medicine (1980) and the Israel Prize, but not the Nobel Prize.
J. Fraser Stoddart, the Scottish-born chemist and Nobel laureate, received both his BSc (1964) and PhD (1966) from the University of Edinburgh.

Robert Burns Woodward was educated at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he received both his bachelor's degree (1936) and his Ph.D. (1937). He was not educated at the University of Edinburgh.

Carolyn R. Bertozzi was awarded both a MacArthur Fellowship (in 1999) and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (in 2022, shared with Morten Meldal and K. Barry Sharpless for the development of click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry).

Roger Adams, the prominent American organic chemist (1889–1971), was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry despite being frequently nominated. He also could not have received a MacArthur Fellowship, as that program was not established until 1981, a decade after his death in 1971.
Rudolph A. Marcus received his B.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees from McGill University in Montreal, Canada, where he studied under Carl A. Winkler.
Robert Burns Woodward received his education from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned both his bachelor's degree (1936) and his PhD (1937), not from McGill University.
Ryōji Noyori was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2001, sharing it with William S. Knowles and K. Barry Sharpless for their work on chirally catalyzed hydrogenation reactions.

Harry B. Gray, the prominent inorganic chemist at Caltech, has received many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, the Priestley Medal, and the National Medal of Science, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Chen Ning Yang was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957, shared with Tsung-Dao Lee, for their work on parity violation in weak interactions.

Victor Frederick Weisskopf, despite being a highly influential theoretical physicist and making major contributions to quantum mechanics and nuclear physics, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received other honors such as the National Medal of Science and the Max Planck Medal, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.

Niklaus Wirth received his Bachelor's degree in Electronics Engineering from ETH Zurich (Swiss Federal Institute of Technology) before going on to further studies at Laval University and UC Berkeley. He later returned to ETH Zurich as a professor.

Dana Scott studied at the University of California, Berkeley (undergraduate) and Princeton University (where he earned his PhD under Alonzo Church). He is not known to have studied at ETH Zurich; his academic career was primarily associated with American institutions such as Princeton, Stanford, and Carnegie Mellon University.
Gérard Debreu was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1983 for his contributions to general equilibrium theory and the rigorous mathematical reformulation of economics.

Dale W. Jorgenson was not awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. He was a distinguished economist known for his work on investment theory and productivity, but he did not receive the Nobel Prize in Economics.

Joseph E. Stiglitz served as Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Clinton (1995–1997) and subsequently as Chief Economist of the World Bank (1997–2000), so he held both positions.

Edmund Phelps did not serve as Chief Economist of the World Bank or as Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers. He spent his career primarily as an academic economist, most notably as a professor at Columbia University, and is best known for his theoretical work on inflation and unemployment, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2006.

Alexander Fleming received his medical education at St Mary's Hospital Medical School in London, not Imperial College London. He also briefly attended the Royal Polytechnic Institution before his medical studies.

Barry Marshall, the Australian physician who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005 for discovering the role of Helicobacter pylori in peptic ulcers, received his medical education at the University of Western Australia, not Imperial College London.

Lotfi Zadeh received his Ph.D. from Columbia University in 1949, and he also worked there as a faculty member before joining UC Berkeley. So yes, he attended Columbia University for his doctoral education.
Marvin Minsky did not attend Columbia University. He studied at Harvard University for his undergraduate degree and received his PhD in mathematics from Princeton University.
Leland H. Hartwell was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001, shared with Tim Hunt and Paul Nurse, for their discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle.

Craig Venter, known for his work on sequencing the human genome and synthetic biology, has not received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While he has received many other honors and awards, the Nobel Prize is not among them.
Alexander Fleming, the Scottish bacteriologist famous for discovering penicillin, served as the Rector of the University of Edinburgh from 1951 to 1954.

Ronald Ross, the Nobel Prize-winning physician known for discovering the role of mosquitoes in transmitting malaria, served as Rector of the University of Edinburgh from 1911 to 1914, having been elected to the position by the student body.
Susumu Tonegawa was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1987 for his discovery of the genetic principle for generation of antibody diversity.

Karl Deisseroth, the neuroscientist known for pioneering optogenetics, has received many prestigious awards (such as the Lasker Award and the Kyoto Prize), but as of my knowledge cutoff he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Luis Walter Alvarez was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1968 for his decisive contributions to elementary particle physics, in particular the discovery of a large number of resonance states, made possible through his development of the technique of using hydrogen bubble chamber and data analysis.

Sidney Drell was a prominent American theoretical physicist, but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He was known for his work in quantum field theory and arms control, and received other honors, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.
Albert Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.

Hermann Weyl was a renowned mathematician and theoretical physicist, but he never received the Nobel Prize in Physics. He is celebrated for his contributions to mathematics, theoretical physics, and philosophy, but the Nobel Prize eluded him.

Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker (1912–2007) was a German physicist and philosopher who was prominently active in philosophy, particularly the philosophy of physics and philosophy of nature. He held a chair in philosophy at the University of Hamburg and wrote extensively on philosophical topics.
Theodore von Kármán was a Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer, and physicist, renowned for his contributions to aerodynamics and astronautics. He was not known as a philosopher.

Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, the French physicist and 1997 Nobel Prize laureate in Physics, did study at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. He also received the CNRS Gold Medal in 1996, one of France's most prestigious scientific awards, the year before he was awarded the Nobel Prize.

Murray Gell-Mann studied at Yale University (undergraduate) and MIT (where he earned his PhD). He did not study at the École Normale Supérieure. Additionally, the CNRS Gold Medal is France's highest scientific honor, typically awarded to researchers with strong ties to French institutions; Gell-Mann did not receive it. His major recognition was the Nobel Prize in Physics (1969).

John Archibald Wheeler was awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1997, recognizing his fundamental contributions to black hole physics, quantum gravity, and general relativity, among other areas of theoretical physics.
Rudolf Peierls was awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1994, recognizing his fundamental contributions to quantum mechanics, solid-state physics, and nuclear physics over his distinguished career.

Oliver E. Williamson, who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009, primarily focused his work on transaction cost economics and the theory of the firm. While contracts and governance structures were related elements of his analysis, his central contributions were about how firms organize transactions and why certain economic activities occur within firms rather than through markets — not contract law itself.

Lawrence Klein was a Nobel Prize-winning economist known for his work on econometric models and macroeconomic forecasting, not contract law. He developed large-scale econometric models to analyze and forecast economic activity.
Karl Ziegler studied chemistry at the University of Marburg, where he earned his PhD in 1920 under the supervision of Karl von Auwers. So yes, he received his education there.

Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff studied at the Delft Polytechnic School, the University of Leiden, the University of Bonn (under Kekulé), and the University of Paris (under Wurtz), and received his doctorate from the University of Utrecht in 1874. The University of Marburg was not part of his education.

Karl Ziegler, the German chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1963, was indeed awarded the Liebig Medal by the German Chemical Society (Gesellschaft Deutscher Chemiker), one of the prestigious recognitions he received during his distinguished career in organometallic chemistry and polymer science.

Based on my knowledge, Manfred Eigen, the German biophysical chemist who won the 1967 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is not known to have been awarded the Liebig Medal. He received numerous other honors, but the Liebig Medal is not among the awards commonly associated with him.
Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1957 for his work on nucleotides and nucleotide co-enzymes.

Frederick Abel (1827–1902) was a distinguished British chemist known for his work on explosives and co-inventing cordite, but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The first Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff in 1901, and Abel was not among the early laureates before his death in 1902.

Albert Einstein formulated both the special theory of relativity (1905) and the general theory of relativity (1915). He studied at ETH Zurich (the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology), where he received his diploma in 1900. Both facts are correct.

Paul Dirac did not formulate the theory of relativity; that was Albert Einstein. Dirac is known for the Dirac equation, his contributions to quantum mechanics, and predicting antimatter. Additionally, Dirac was educated at the University of Bristol and then the University of Cambridge, not ETH Zurich (which is associated with Einstein).
Freeman Dyson received the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1981, recognized for his contributions to quantum field theory and other areas of theoretical physics.
Mildred Dresselhaus received the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1992, shared with Paul Chaikin, for her research on the electronic properties of semimetals and carbon-based materials.
Niels Bohr was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922 for his work on the structure of atoms and the radiation emanating from them.

Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered pulsars as a graduate student, but the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for that discovery was awarded to her supervisor Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, not to her. This omission became one of the most controversial decisions in Nobel Prize history.

Alexander Prokhorov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1964, sharing it with Nikolay Basov and Charles Townes for fundamental work in quantum electronics leading to the development of masers and lasers.
Nikolay Nikolayevich Semyonov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1956 (shared with Cyril Hinshelwood) for his work on the mechanism of chemical reactions, not the Nobel Prize in Physics.

James D. Watson attended the University of Chicago, where he received his Bachelor of Science degree in 1947 at the age of 19, having enrolled in the university's experimental college program at age 15.

Selman Waksman did not pursue his education at the University of Chicago. He earned his B.S. from Rutgers College in 1915 and his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley in 1918. He later spent most of his career at Rutgers University.

Louis Agassiz specialized in both ichthyology (his landmark work on fossil fish) and glaciology (his ice age theory). Additionally, he studied at the University of Zurich (1824–1825) and at Heidelberg University (1826) as part of his academic training before completing his doctorate in Munich. Any one of these conditions alone would satisfy the 'or' in the question.

Richard Owen (1804–1892) was a comparative anatomist and paleontologist, best known for coining the term 'dinosaur.' He was neither an ichthyologist nor a glaciologist. His education was in medicine and anatomy, studied at Edinburgh and completed in London — not at Heidelberg University or the University of Zurich.
Edmund Phelps studied at both institutions. He completed his undergraduate degree at Amherst College and then earned his Ph.D. in economics at Yale University.

Robert Mundell studied at the University of British Columbia, the University of Washington, and the London School of Economics, before earning his PhD from MIT. He did not study at Yale University or Amherst College.

Rudolf Mössbauer was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1961, shared with Robert Hofstadter, for his research on the recoil-free resonance absorption of gamma radiation, known as the Mössbauer effect.

Rudolf Peierls, the British theoretical physicist known for his contributions to quantum mechanics, solid-state physics, and nuclear physics (including the Frisch-Peierls memorandum), was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received many honors, including a knighthood, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.
Leon Max Lederman received the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1982, which he shared with Martin Perl, for their contributions to lepton physics. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1988.

Ernest Lawrence did not receive the Wolf Prize in Physics. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for the invention of the cyclotron. The Wolf Prize was not established until 1978, and Lawrence died in 1958, making it impossible for him to have received it.

Samuel J. Danishefsky received the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2016, shared with Stuart L. Schreiber, in recognition of his contributions to organic synthesis and the development of new methods for the synthesis of complex natural products and anticancer agents.
George M. Whitesides was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2018, recognizing his pioneering contributions to chemistry, including work on self-assembly, soft lithography, and microfluidics.
Richard Smalley was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996, along with Robert Curl and Harold Kroto, for their discovery of fullerenes (buckminsterfullerene, C60).

Harry B. Gray, the prominent inorganic chemist at Caltech, has received many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, the Priestley Medal, and the National Medal of Science, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Jean Tirole, the French economist and 2014 Nobel laureate in Economics, is not known to have received a Guggenheim Fellowship. His notable awards include the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, the CNRS Gold Medal, and various other economics prizes, but a Guggenheim Fellowship is not among the recognitions typically associated with him.

Daron Acemoglu, the MIT economist, has received numerous prestigious awards throughout his career, including a Guggenheim Fellowship, in addition to honors such as the John Bates Clark Medal and eventually the Nobel Prize in Economics (2024).

Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker attended both the University of Göttingen and Leipzig University as part of his education in physics. He studied under Werner Heisenberg at Leipzig, among other institutions.

Rashid Sunyaev received his education in the Soviet Union. He studied at the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (MIPT/Phystech) and conducted his graduate work under Yakov Zel'dovich in Moscow. He did not attend the University of Göttingen or Leipzig University, which are German institutions.

James Heckman was awarded the John Bates Clark Medal in 1983 by the American Economic Association, recognizing his significant contributions to economic thought. He later also received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2000.

Alvin E. Roth, while a Nobel Prize laureate in Economics (2012, shared with Lloyd Shapley), is not known to have been awarded the John Bates Clark Medal, which is given to an American economist under the age of 40 who has made significant contributions to economic thought.
Henri Becquerel attended the École polytechnique, entering in 1872, before continuing his studies at the École des Ponts et Chaussées.
Serge Haroche, the French physicist and 2012 Nobel Prize laureate, attended the École normale supérieure, not the École polytechnique.

Ahmed H. Zewail was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1999 for his studies of the transition states of chemical reactions using femtosecond spectroscopy, making him the founder of femtochemistry.
Albert Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921, not Chemistry. The prize was given for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.

Pavel Alekseyevich Cherenkov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1958, sharing it with Ilya Frank and Igor Tamm, for the discovery and interpretation of the Cherenkov effect (Cherenkov radiation).

Yakov Borisovich Zel'dovich, despite his enormous contributions to nuclear physics, astrophysics, and cosmology, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received the Hero of Socialist Labour three times and the Lenin Prize, among other Soviet honors, but he died in 1987 without receiving the Nobel Prize.
Murray Gell-Mann studied at both institutions. He received his bachelor's degree from Yale University in 1948 and then earned his PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1951.

Enrico Fermi did not study at Yale University or MIT. He received his education in Italy, earning his doctorate from the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa in 1922. He later did postdoctoral work in Germany and the Netherlands before becoming a professor in Rome and eventually joining the University of Chicago in the United States.
Anthony Fauci was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Joe Biden in December 2022, recognizing his decades of service in infectious disease research and public health.

Joan Steitz, the renowned biochemist known for her work on RNA, has received many prestigious awards including the Lasker Award and the Gairdner International Award, but I do not have reliable information indicating she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Johann Friedrich Gmelin (1748–1804) was a German naturalist who worked across several fields, including as an entomologist. He contributed to the 13th edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae, cataloguing numerous insect species among others. He is not particularly noted as a mycologist.

Gottlieb Conrad Christian Storr (1749–1821) was a German physician and naturalist primarily known for his work in zoology, particularly the systematics of vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles). He is not recognized as having pursued work specifically as an entomologist (insect specialist) or as a mycologist (fungus specialist).

Daniel Kahneman is a renowned psychologist and behavioral economist, widely known for his work on cognitive biases and prospect theory. He held positions as a professor of psychology at multiple universities and won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, largely based on his psychological research.

Angus Deaton is a Scottish-American economist, not a psychologist. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 2015 for his analysis of consumption, poverty, and welfare. His entire academic career has been in economics, at institutions such as Cambridge, Bristol, and Princeton.
Niklaus Wirth designed and developed the Pascal programming language, which was released in 1970. It was named after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal.

Pascal was invented by Niklaus Wirth, not Edsger W. Dijkstra. Dijkstra is known for contributions such as Dijkstra's algorithm, the concept of structured programming, and the semaphore concept for concurrent programming.
Manfred Eigen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1967, sharing it with Ronald Norrish and George Porter for their studies of extremely fast chemical reactions.

Hans Bethe was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1967, not in Chemistry. He received it for his contributions to the theory of nuclear reactions, especially his discoveries concerning the energy production in stars.
Herbert C. Brown received both his B.S. (1936) and his Ph.D. (1938) from the University of Chicago, so he completed a significant portion of his formal education there.

George Andrew Olah completed his education in Hungary, receiving his undergraduate degree and Ph.D. from the Technical University of Budapest (now Budapest University of Technology and Economics). He had no educational ties to the University of Chicago.

Barbara McClintock studied at Cornell University, where she earned her B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. in botany. She later worked at the University of Missouri as a faculty member, but her studies were conducted at Cornell.
Oliver Smithies studied at the University of Oxford, where he earned his BA and DPhil degrees. He did not study at Cornell University or the University of Missouri.

Louis Agassiz made major contributions to both glaciology (his glacier theory and studies of ice ages) and ichthyology (his extensive work on fossil and living fish, including his multi-volume 'Recherches sur les poissons fossiles').

Jane Goodall is renowned for her research on chimpanzees and primatology, as well as her work in conservation and animal behavior. Her scientific career did not involve glaciology (the study of glaciers) or ichthyology (the study of fish).
J. J. Thomson, the British physicist who discovered the electron, was awarded the Copley Medal by the Royal Society in 1914, in addition to his Nobel Prize in Physics (1906) and other honors.

Edward Victor Appleton, the British physicist known for his work on the ionosphere and recipient of the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physics, was not awarded the Copley Medal. He received other honors such as a knighthood and the Royal Medal, but the Copley Medal was not among his awards.

Philippe Aghion received his education at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris and earned his PhD from MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), not Harvard University. He has been a professor at Harvard, but that is his professional affiliation, not his educational background.
Edmund Phelps did not attend Harvard University. He completed his undergraduate studies at Amherst College and received his PhD in economics from Yale University.
Walter Gilbert was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980, shared with Frederick Sanger and Paul Berg, for his contributions to the determination of base sequences in nucleic acids.

Günter Blobel was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1999 for his discovery that proteins have intrinsic signals that govern their transport and localization in the cell. He did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Erwin Schrödinger was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1933, sharing it with Paul Dirac, for the discovery of new productive forms of atomic theory.
Walter Kohn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998 (shared with John Pople), not the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received it for his development of density-functional theory.
Melvin Calvin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1961 for his research on the carbon dioxide assimilation in plants, now known as the Calvin cycle.

Isabella Karle was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Her husband, Jerome Karle, shared the 1985 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Herbert Hauptman for the development of direct methods for the determination of crystal structures, but Isabella Karle herself did not receive the prize despite her significant contributions to the field of X-ray crystallography.

Lawrence Klein was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1980 for the creation of econometric models and their application to the analysis of economic fluctuations and economic policies.

Martin Feldstein, the prominent American economist and Harvard professor, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Despite being widely regarded as a potential candidate, he passed away in June 2019 without receiving the prize.
Leland H. Hartwell earned his Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1964, so he did indeed pursue graduate studies there.

Edward B. Lewis, the Nobel Prize-winning geneticist, did his undergraduate studies at the University of Minnesota and earned his PhD from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), where he also spent his entire academic career. There is no record of him pursuing studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Enrico Fermi was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1938 for his demonstrations of the existence of new radioactive elements produced by neutron irradiation, and for his related discovery of nuclear reactions brought about by slow neutrons.

Mildred Dresselhaus, often called the 'Queen of Carbon Science,' received many prestigious honors including the National Medal of Science, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and the Kavli Prize, but she was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Charles Townes attended the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), where he earned his Ph.D. in physics in 1939. Before Caltech, he had completed his undergraduate studies at Furman University and his master's degree at Duke University.

Carl Wieman received his B.S. from MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) and his Ph.D. from Stanford University. He did not attend the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) for his education.

Rudolph A. Marcus was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1984/1985, shared with Henry Taube, for his contributions to the theory of electron transfer reactions. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1992 for the same work.

Robert S. Mulliken was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1966 for his work on chemical bonds and the electronic structure of molecules by the molecular orbital method. However, he was not awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, which began in 1978.

Selman Waksman received his B.S. degree from Rutgers College (now Rutgers University) in 1915, and he later spent the majority of his academic career there as a professor and researcher, eventually winning the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1952.

Stanley B. Prusiner was educated at the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned both his undergraduate degree in chemistry and his MD from the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine. He was not educated at Rutgers University.

Ahmed H. Zewail, the Egyptian-American chemist who won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on femtochemistry, received many prestigious awards, but the Priestley Medal (the highest honor of the American Chemical Society) is not among the awards commonly associated with him in available records.

Ernest Rutherford did not receive the Priestley Medal. The Priestley Medal is the highest honor of the American Chemical Society. Rutherford's notable awards include the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1908), the Copley Medal, and he was made a Baron, but the Priestley Medal was not among his honors.
Karl Alexander Müller, along with Johannes Georg Bednorz, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1987 for their discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in ceramic materials.

Peter Zoller, the Austrian theoretical physicist known for his work in quantum optics and quantum information, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He has received other prestigious awards such as the Dirac Medal and the Wolf Prize, but not the Nobel Prize.

William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, both served as President of the Royal Society (1890–1895) and became a member of the House of Lords when he was elevated to the peerage as Baron Kelvin of Largs in 1892, entitling him to sit in the House of Lords.

James Hopwood Jeans (1877–1946) was a distinguished British physicist and astronomer who was knighted in 1928 and was a Fellow of the Royal Society, but he never served as its President. LaTeX was developed by Leslie Lamport in the early 1980s. The name 'LaTeX' is derived from 'Lamport TeX,' as it is a document preparation system built on top of Donald Knuth's TeX typesetting system.

Maurice Vincent Wilkes was a British computer scientist known for developing EDSAC and the concept of microprogramming. LaTeX was developed by Leslie Lamport in the 1980s, based on Donald Knuth's TeX typesetting system.

Saul Perlmutter attended Harvard University for his undergraduate education and received his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. Riccardo Giacconi received his doctorate from the University of Milan (1954). John A. Pople, the British theoretical chemist and Nobel laureate, was awarded the Davy Medal by the Royal Society in 1988 for his contributions to theoretical and computational chemistry.

Harold Kroto was awarded the Davy Medal by the Royal Society in 1990, along with Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, for their discovery of buckminsterfullerene (C60). They later shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996 for the same work.
Enrico Fermi received the Matteucci Medal in 1926, awarded by the Italian National Academy of Sciences. There is no strong evidence that he received the Max Planck Medal.

Steven Weinberg received the Max Planck Medal, awarded by the German Physical Society, in 1986, in recognition of his outstanding contributions to theoretical physics, including his work on the electroweak unification theory.

Robert Brown (1773–1858), the Scottish botanist famous for discovering Brownian motion, trained in medicine at the University of Edinburgh and served as a surgeon's mate in the British Army before pursuing his career in botany.

George Bentham (1800–1884) was a prominent British botanist, best known for his work on plant taxonomy and his collaboration with Joseph Dalton Hooker on 'Genera Plantarum.' He was not a surgeon; early in his career he worked in a legal capacity before devoting himself entirely to botany.
Glenn T. Seaborg received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1951, which he shared with Edwin McMillan, for their discoveries in the chemistry of the transuranium elements.

Roger Adams was a highly distinguished American organic chemist known for the Adams catalyst and other contributions, but he never received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, despite being nominated multiple times.
Dudley R. Herschbach received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1986, sharing it with Yuan T. Lee and John C. Polanyi for their contributions to the dynamics of chemical elementary processes.

Gabor A. Somorjai, the renowned surface chemist at UC Berkeley, has not received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he is widely regarded as a leading figure in surface science and catalysis and has received many prestigious awards, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry is not among them.

Arthur Kornberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1959, which he shared with Severo Ochoa, for their discovery of the mechanisms in the biological synthesis of ribonucleic acid and deoxyribonucleic acid.

Britton Chance, the renowned American biophysicist and biochemist, was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Although he made significant contributions to enzyme kinetics, biophysics, and biochemistry and was frequently considered a Nobel candidate, he never received the prize.
Roger D. Kornberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2006 for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription.

Stephen J. Benkovic, while a highly distinguished biochemist known for his work in enzymology and bioorganic chemistry and the recipient of many honors (including the National Medal of Science), has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Linus Pauling was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. He is one of the very few individuals to have received two Nobel Prizes, having also won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954.

Mario J. Molina was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995 (shared with F. Sherwood Rowland and Paul Crutzen) for his work on the depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer, not the Nobel Peace Prize.

Sir Alan Battersby, the distinguished British chemist known for his work on biosynthesis of natural products, received several prestigious awards including the Davy Medal and the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, but he did not receive the Copley Medal.

Harry B. Gray is a highly decorated chemist who has received many prestigious awards (including the National Medal of Science, the Priestley Medal, and the Wolf Prize in Chemistry), but the Copley Medal—awarded by the Royal Society of London—is not among his known honors.
David Baltimore did attend MIT. He began his graduate studies there before completing his PhD at Rockefeller University. He also later joined MIT's faculty and was a professor there for many years.

Arthur Kornberg attended the City College of New York for his undergraduate studies and earned his medical degree from the University of Rochester School of Medicine. He did not attend the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
George M. Whitesides received his Ph.D. from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in 1964, where he conducted his doctoral research under the supervision of John D. Roberts.

Jennifer Doudna did not attend the California Institute of Technology. She received her undergraduate degree from Pomona College and her Ph.D. from Harvard University, where she worked under Jack Szostak.

Peter Debye (Peter Debije) studied electrical engineering at RWTH Aachen University (Technische Hochschule Aachen), graduating in 1905. Glenn T. Seaborg studied at UCLA for his undergraduate degree and earned his PhD from UC Berkeley. He never attended RWTH Aachen University or ETH Zurich. Werner Heisenberg studied physics at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München under Arnold Sommerfeld, where he earned his doctorate in 1923. He also studied at the University of Göttingen under Max Born, but Munich was a key institution in his education.
Erwin Schrödinger received his education at the University of Vienna, where he completed his doctorate in 1910. He did not study at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München.

Carl Wieman did not study at Princeton or Cornell University. He received his undergraduate degree from MIT and his PhD from Stanford University.

Peter Debije (Peter Debye) was awarded the National Medal of Science in 1965 by President Lyndon B. Johnson, recognizing his outstanding contributions to physics and chemistry, including his work on molecular dipole moments and X-ray diffraction.

Otto Hahn was a German chemist who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1944 for the discovery of nuclear fission. The National Medal of Science is a United States award, and Otto Hahn, being a German scientist, was not a recipient of it.

Zhores Ivanovich Alferov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000 (shared with Herbert Kroemer and Jack Kilby) for developing semiconductor heterostructures. Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov (1903–1987) was a renowned Soviet mathematician, but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (there is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics, and he did not receive the Physics prize). John Cockcroft was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1951, shared with Ernest Walton, for their pioneer work on the transmutation of atomic nuclei by artificially accelerated atomic particles.

William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin (Lord Kelvin), despite being one of the most influential physicists of the 19th century, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Although the Nobel Prize in Physics began in 1901 (six years before his death in 1907), he was not among its recipients.
Jean Tirole, the French economist and Nobel Prize laureate, earned his PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1981, so yes, he studied there.
Edmund Phelps received his undergraduate degree from Amherst College and his PhD in economics from Yale University. He did not study at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Yakov Borisovich Zel'dovich was named a Hero of Socialist Labour three times (in 1949, 1953, and 1956) for his contributions to Soviet nuclear weapons development and scientific research. Ludvig Faddeev was a distinguished Soviet/Russian mathematical physicist who received honors such as the Lenin Prize and the Max Planck Medal, but he was not awarded the Bruce Medal (an astronomy award given by the Astronomical Society of the Pacific) nor was he named a Hero of Socialist Labour.
George Gabriel Stokes held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at Cambridge University from 1849 until his death in 1903, one of the longest tenures in the history of that chair.

Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh) held the Cavendish Professorship of Physics at Cambridge (1879–1884), not the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics. The Lucasian Chair during much of his era was held by George Gabriel Stokes and later Joseph Larmor.
Harold Kroto (Sir Harold Walter Kroto) received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996, shared with Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, for their discovery of fullerenes (buckminsterfullerene, C60).

Allen J. Bard, despite being a highly acclaimed electrochemist and frequent Nobel Prize candidate who received many prestigious awards (including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2008 and the National Medal of Science), did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Christos Papadimitriou was awarded the Knuth Prize in 2002 for his outstanding contributions to the foundations of computer science, particularly in computational complexity theory, algorithms, and game theory.

Éva Tardos, a Hungarian-American computer scientist at Cornell University known for her work in algorithms and algorithmic game theory, was awarded the Knuth Prize in 2019 for her fundamental contributions to combinatorial optimization and algorithmic game theory.

Georges Cuvier held a professorship at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle starting in 1795 and served in a leading administrative/directorial capacity there. Alcide d'Orbigny held a chair of paleontology at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle from 1853 until his death in 1857, but he did not serve as its director. Noga Alon received the Shaw Prize in Mathematical Sciences in 2022, shared with Ehud Hrushovski, for their contributions to discrete mathematics and model theory respectively.
Saharon Shelah received the Shaw Prize in Mathematical Sciences in 2009, recognized for his work in mathematical logic, particularly in model theory and set theory.

Alexander R. Todd was created Baron Todd of Trumpington in 1962, which gave him a seat in the House of Lords as a life peer. He served as a member of the House of Lords following his elevation to the peerage.

John Charles Polanyi is a Hungarian-Canadian chemist and Nobel Prize winner who has been a professor at the University of Toronto. He has never served as a member of the House of Lords, which is a chamber of the UK Parliament.

John A. Pople, the British theoretical chemist known for his development of computational methods in quantum chemistry, was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (in 1992, shared with Norman Allinger). He later also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998.

Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd is primarily known for receiving the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1957 for his work on nucleotides and nucleotide co-enzymes. There is no record in my knowledge of him being awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, which has been awarded since 1978.
Selman Waksman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1952 for his discovery of streptomycin, the first antibiotic effective against tuberculosis.

Craig Venter, known for his work on sequencing the human genome and synthetic biology, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While he has received numerous other awards, the Nobel Prize is not among them.

K. C. Nicolaou completed postdoctoral research at Harvard University, working in the laboratory of Nobel laureate E. J. Corey, after earning his PhD from University College London. Postdoctoral training is generally considered part of a researcher's education and academic formation.
Harold Kroto completed his undergraduate and doctoral education at the University of Sheffield in the United Kingdom. He did not attend Harvard University at any stage of his education.

John Cornforth (Sir John Warcup Cornforth), the Australian-British chemist and Nobel Prize laureate, studied at the University of Oxford, where he completed his DPhil after initially graduating from the University of Sydney.

James Fraser Stoddart received his BSc (1964) and PhD (1966) from the University of Edinburgh, not the University of Oxford. Otto Hahn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1944 for his discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei (nuclear fission).

Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov, the prominent Soviet geometer known for his contributions to convex geometry and the foundations of geometry, was awarded the Lobachevsky Prize in recognition of his outstanding work in geometry, consistent with the prize's focus on significant contributions to geometry in the tradition of Lobachevsky.

Israel Gelfand, the prominent Soviet-American mathematician, was indeed awarded the Lobachevsky Prize, which is given by the Russian (formerly Soviet) Academy of Sciences for outstanding contributions to geometry and related areas. William Crookes, the British chemist and physicist known for his discovery of thallium and invention of the Crookes tube, was indeed awarded the Elliott Cresson Medal by the Franklin Institute, recognizing his significant contributions to science.

Martin Chalfie attended Harvard University, where he received his undergraduate degree (B.A.) in 1969 and later his Ph.D. in 1977. He is best known for his work on green fluorescent protein (GFP), for which he shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Peter Zoller, the Austrian theoretical physicist known for his work in quantum optics and quantum information, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He has received other prestigious awards such as the Dirac Medal and the Wolf Prize in Physics, but not the Nobel Prize.

Luis Walter Alvarez received his education at the University of Chicago, earning his BS in 1932 and his PhD in 1936. He did not pursue education at Leipzig University.

Rudolf Mössbauer received numerous prestigious awards, most notably the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1961 for his discovery of the Mössbauer effect. Herbert C. Brown was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1979, which he shared with Georg Wittig, for his development of the use of boron-containing compounds in organic synthesis (hydroboration).

Allen J. Bard, the renowned electrochemist, did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Carl Bosch, the German chemist known for the Haber-Bosch process and Nobel Prize laureate in Chemistry (1931), is not known to have been awarded the Goethe Prize. His notable honors include the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, but the Goethe Prize is not among the awards typically associated with him.

Luis Walter Alvarez received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1968 for his decisive contributions to elementary particle physics, in particular the discovery of a large number of resonance states, made possible through his development of the technique of using hydrogen bubble chamber and data analysis.

John Archibald Wheeler, despite his major contributions to theoretical physics including coining the term 'black hole' and his work on general relativity and nuclear physics, never received the Nobel Prize in Physics. This is widely considered one of the notable omissions in Nobel Prize history.

Ilya Prigogine worked professionally as a physical chemist and thermodynamicist (with work closely related to physics) at the Université Libre de Bruxelles and later the University of Texas at Austin, and he also engaged deeply with philosophical questions about time and complexity (co-authoring philosophical works). Sir Derek Barton was a British organic chemist, best known for developing conformational analysis and winning the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1969. Linus Pauling was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. He is one of the few individuals to have won two Nobel Prizes, the other being the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954.

James Fraser Stoddart was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2016 (shared with Jean-Pierre Sauvage and Bernard L. Feringa) for the design and synthesis of molecular machines. He did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

Günter Blobel, the German-American cell biologist, was awarded the King Faisal International Prize in Science in 1996, recognizing his work on protein targeting and transport. He later received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1999 for the same body of work.

Elizabeth Blackburn was awarded the King Faisal International Prize in Science in 2008, recognizing her pioneering work on telomeres and telomerase, the same research that later earned her the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2009.

Werner Heisenberg was awarded the Pour le Mérite (the civil class for Sciences and Arts), a prestigious German order. He was not awarded the Sigmund Freud Prize, which is given by the Deutsche Akademie für Sprache und Dichtung for scientific prose writing.

Wolfgang Pauli was awarded the Pour le Mérite (specifically the Pour le Mérite for Sciences and Arts, the peace class of the Prussian order), recognizing his outstanding contributions to theoretical physics. Oliver Smithies was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2007, shared with Mario Capecchi and Martin Evans, for their discoveries of principles for introducing specific gene modifications in mice by the use of embryonic stem cells.

Craig Venter, known for his work on sequencing the human genome and creating synthetic life, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While he is widely regarded as a pioneer in genomics, he has not received a Nobel Prize.
Edmund Phelps pursued his education at both institutions. He completed his undergraduate studies at Amherst College and then earned his PhD in economics from Yale University.

Wassily Leontief pursued his education at the University of Leningrad (now St. Petersburg State University) and then received his PhD from the University of Berlin in 1928. He did not attend Yale University or Amherst College.

Harold Clayton Urey received his bachelor's degree from the University of Montana and his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. He was later a faculty member at Columbia University, where he discovered deuterium, but he was not educated there as a student.

Gerhard Herzberg received his education in Germany, earning his doctorate from the Darmstadt University of Technology (Technische Hochschule Darmstadt) in 1928. He was not educated at Columbia University.
Robert Robinson, the British organic chemist, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1947 for his investigations on plant products of biological importance, especially the alkaloids.

Allen J. Bard, while a highly acclaimed electrochemist who received numerous prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2008) and the National Medal of Science, was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Oliver Smithies was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 2002, shared with Mario Capecchi, for their work on gene targeting in mice. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2007 for the same body of work.

Robert F. Furchgott was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1998, shared with Louis Ignarro and Ferid Murad, for their discoveries related to nitric oxide as a signaling molecule in the cardiovascular system. They subsequently also received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1998.
Max Planck received the Goethe Prize in 1945, awarded by the city of Frankfurt. He did not receive the Copley Medal (a Royal Society award).

Louis-Victor de Broglie, the French physicist famous for his theory of wave-particle duality, received the Nobel Prize in Physics (1929) among other honors, but he did not receive either the Copley Medal (awarded by the Royal Society) or the Goethe Prize (awarded by the city of Frankfurt).

Michael O. Rabin is best known for receiving the Turing Award in 1976 (shared with Dana Scott) for his contributions to the theory of nondeterministic automata. He has not been awarded the Wolf Prize in Mathematics, which has recognized other mathematicians in its history.

Richard Karp was awarded the Wolf Prize in Mathematics in 2016, sharing the prize with László Lovász, in recognition of their contributions to the foundations of computer science and discrete mathematics.
Leonid Hurwicz studied law at the University of Warsaw, earning his law degree there before going on to study economics at other institutions such as the London School of Economics.

George Akerlof received his undergraduate degree from Yale University and his PhD from MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) in 1966. He has no known educational connection to the University of Warsaw.
Richard Feynman attended Princeton University for his graduate studies, earning his PhD in physics in 1942 under the supervision of John Archibald Wheeler.

Murray Gell-Mann attended MIT for his undergraduate studies and received his PhD from MIT as well — actually he got his bachelor's from Yale and his PhD from MIT. He did not attend Princeton University.

Paul Dirac held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge from 1932 to 1969, one of the most prestigious mathematics chairs in the world, previously held by Isaac Newton and later by Stephen Hawking.

Roger Penrose did not hold the Lucasian Professorship. He held the Rouse Ball Professorship of Mathematics at the University of Oxford. The Lucasian Chair is associated with figures such as Isaac Newton, Paul Dirac, and Stephen Hawking, among others.

Irving Langmuir was awarded the Priestley Medal, the highest honor of the American Chemical Society, in 1950, recognizing his distinguished contributions to chemistry.

Adolf Butenandt was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1939 (shared with Leopold Ruzicka) for his work on sex hormones, including isolating and characterizing estrone, androsterone, and progesterone. Otto Heinrich Warburg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1931 for his discovery of the nature and mode of action of the respiratory enzyme, not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Robert Burns Woodward received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1965 for his outstanding achievements in the art of organic synthesis.

Allen J. Bard, the renowned electrochemist, did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he was highly decorated—winning the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2008) and the National Medal of Science, among other honors—he was not awarded the Nobel Prize before his death in February 2024.

James Hector (1834–1907) was trained as a physician and surgeon, and he did practice surgery — most notably serving as the surgeon-geologist on the Palliser Expedition (1857–1860) in western Canada. He also played a central role in the New Zealand Institute (the predecessor to the Royal Society of New Zealand), serving as its long-time manager and editor of its Transactions, and is associated with leadership positions in that body. Charles Darwin never practiced as a surgeon; he briefly studied medicine at Edinburgh University but abandoned it to pursue natural history. Claude Louis Berthollet was a French chemist who initially trained in medicine and received a medical degree. He practiced as a physician early in his career before becoming more focused on chemistry, for which he is primarily remembered.

Marcellin Berthelot (1827–1907) was a prominent French chemist, not a physician. He is renowned for his contributions to organic chemistry and thermochemistry, including early work on organic synthesis, and he also served as a statesman in France. He did not pursue medicine or practice as a doctor.
Joseph E. Stiglitz served as the Chief Economist and Senior Vice President of the World Bank from 1997 to 2000, before being awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2001.

Lawrence Klein, the Nobel Prize-winning economist (1980), was primarily known as a professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School and for his work on econometric models. Jennifer Doudna was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020, along with Emmanuelle Charpentier, for the development of CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology.

Francis Crick was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, shared with James Watson and Maurice Wilkins, for their discovery of the double helix structure of DNA. He did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Leon Lederman received the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1982, shared with Martin Perl, before he went on to receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1988.
Steven Weinberg received the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1979, sharing it with Sheldon Glashow, recognizing their contributions to the unification of the weak and electromagnetic interactions.

Louis-Victor de Broglie received numerous honors, most notably the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1929 for his discovery of the wave nature of electrons. Anne L'Huillier, the French-Swedish physicist who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics, is not known to have received the CNRS Gold Medal. John Cockcroft studied mathematics at the Victoria University of Manchester before going on to St John's College, Cambridge. He studied there under mathematician Horace Lamb, among others.

Peter Higgs attended King's College London, where he earned his BSc, MSc, and PhD. He did not attend the Victoria University of Manchester. He is most associated with the University of Edinburgh, where he spent the majority of his academic career.

Maurice Wilkins was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, sharing it with Francis Crick and James Watson for their discoveries concerning the molecular structure of nucleic acids (DNA).

John Kendrew was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1962 (shared with Max Perutz) for his work on determining the three-dimensional structure of myoglobin, not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Cyril Norman Hinshelwood studied at Balliol College, University of Oxford, where he later became a fellow and conducted his Nobel Prize-winning research on chemical reaction kinetics.

Robert Robinson (1886–1975), the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, studied at the University of Manchester, where he earned his BSc and DSc under William Henry Perkin Jr. He later held the Waynflete Professorship of Chemistry at the University of Oxford (1930–1955), but as a professor, not as a student.

Freeman Dyson attended both institutions. He studied mathematics at the University of Cambridge (Trinity College) and later went to Cornell University as a graduate student, where he worked with Hans Bethe.

Victor Frederick Weisskopf did not attend Cornell University or the University of Cambridge. He studied physics in Europe, receiving his PhD from the University of Göttingen in 1931. He later worked at institutions such as MIT, but his education was primarily at European universities.
Emmanuelle Charpentier, along with Jennifer Doudna, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for the development of a method for genome editing (CRISPR-Cas9).

Britton Chance, the American biophysicist known for his work on enzyme kinetics and biological spectroscopy, did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he was a highly acclaimed scientist who received numerous honors, the Nobel Prize was not among them.

Bernhard Schölkopf, the renowned machine learning researcher known for his work on kernel methods and causality, received the Körber European Science Prize in 2019 for his contributions to machine learning and artificial intelligence research.

Klaus-Robert Müller, a German computer scientist known for his contributions to machine learning and explainable AI, received the Körber European Science Prize in 2019 for his work on making artificial intelligence more interpretable and transparent.

Harold Kroto, the British chemist who co-discovered fullerenes and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996, was not awarded the Copley Medal. While he received numerous honors, the Copley Medal is not among them.

Ahmed Zewail, the Egyptian-American chemist known as the 'father of femtochemistry,' received numerous prestigious awards including the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1999), but he was not awarded the Copley Medal, which is given by the Royal Society of London.
Vint Cerf, along with Bob Kahn, received the ACM Turing Award in 2004 for their foundational work on the design and implementation of the Internet's core communications protocols (TCP/IP).

Charles K. Kao received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009 for his pioneering work on fiber optics, but he did not receive the Turing Award, which is given by the ACM for contributions to computer science.
Hans Bethe was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1967 for his contributions to the theory of nuclear reactions, especially his discoveries concerning the energy production in stars.

Jocelyn Bell Burnell was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Yuan T. Lee, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, received his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley in 1965, and later served as a professor there.

Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd, was educated at the University of Glasgow, then received his PhD from the University of Frankfurt, and subsequently worked at Oxford, the University of Edinburgh, the Lister Institute, the University of Manchester, and Cambridge University. Luc Montagnier was a French virologist best known for co-discovering HIV, primarily associated with the Pasteur Institute in Paris. He was never the President of Rockefeller University. Karl Ernst von Baer, the Estonian-German naturalist and founder of modern embryology, received the Copley Medal from the Royal Society of London in 1867, in recognition of his outstanding contributions to science, particularly his work on embryonic development.

Hermann Burmeister was a notable German-Argentine naturalist and entomologist, but he is not recorded among the recipients of the Copley Medal, which is awarded by the Royal Society of London for outstanding scientific achievement.

Karl Deisseroth is an MD-PhD who practices psychiatry and is a professor of bioengineering and psychiatry at Stanford University. He completed both his graduate studies and medical training associated with Stanford, and he is best known for co-developing optogenetics.

Paul Nurse is a British biochemist and cell biologist, not a psychiatrist. He is known for his work on cell cycle regulation, for which he won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001. Angus Deaton studied at the University of Cambridge, where he received his BA, MA, and PhD from Fitzwilliam College. Cambridge was central to his academic formation before he went on to hold positions at other institutions like Princeton University.
Paul Samuelson received his education at the University of Chicago (undergraduate) and Harvard University (where he earned his PhD). He was not educated at the University of Cambridge.
Robert Solow received the John Bates Clark Medal in 1961, awarded by the American Economic Association to an economist under 40 who has made significant contributions to economic thought.

Philippe Aghion, the French economist known for his work on endogenous growth theory, did not receive the John Bates Clark Medal. He has received other honors, such as the BBVA Frontiers of Knowledge Award and the Princess of Asturias Award (shared with Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson in 2021), but not the Clark Medal.

Sir Derek Barton, the British chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1969, received numerous honors including the Davy Medal, but he was not awarded the Copley Medal, which is one of the Royal Society's highest honors typically given to different recipients.

Harold Clayton Urey, the American physical chemist known for discovering deuterium and awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1934, received numerous honors including the Priestley Medal and the National Medal of Science, but the Copley Medal (awarded by the Royal Society) is not among his noted awards.

Irving Langmuir received his Ph.D. from the University of Göttingen in 1906, where he studied under the physical chemist Walther Nernst. Before that, he had earned his undergraduate degree in metallurgical engineering from Columbia University's School of Mines in 1903.

Glenn T. Seaborg was educated at UCLA (University of California, Los Angeles) for his undergraduate degree and received his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. He was not educated at the University of Göttingen.

Robert Robinson, the British organic chemist, received the Copley Medal from the Royal Society in 1942, in recognition of his distinguished contributions to chemistry, particularly his work on plant pigments, alkaloids, and other natural products.

Alan MacDiarmid, the New Zealand-born chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2000 for his work on conductive polymers, did not receive the Copley Medal. The Copley Medal is awarded by the Royal Society of London, and MacDiarmid is not among its recipients.

James Fraser Stoddart, the Scottish chemist who won the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on molecular machines, is not known to have received the Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology. Ahmed H. Zewail was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1999 for his pioneering work in femtochemistry, but he is not known to have received the Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology, which is awarded by the Foresight Institute for advances in nanotechnology.
Alexander R. Todd was created Baron Todd of Trumpington in 1962, which granted him a life peerage and membership in the House of Lords, where he served as a crossbench peer.

Max Perutz, the Nobel Prize-winning molecular biologist, was honored with many distinctions including the Companion of Honour, but he was not elevated to the peerage and did not serve as a member of the House of Lords.
Walter Kohn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998, sharing it with John Pople, for his development of density-functional theory.
Klaus von Klitzing was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1985 for the discovery of the quantized Hall effect, not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1944 for his discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei (nuclear fission).

Victor Frederick Weisskopf was a renowned theoretical physicist who made major contributions to quantum mechanics and nuclear physics, but he did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (or in any category).
Gerhard Herzberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1971 for his contributions to the knowledge of the electronic structure and geometry of molecules, particularly free radicals.

Richard Zare, the Stanford chemist known for his work in laser chemistry and chemical analysis, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he is highly accomplished and has received numerous other honors, he is not a Nobel laureate.

Israel Gelfand, despite lacking a formal undergraduate degree, was admitted to graduate school at Lomonosov Moscow State University, where he studied under Andrei Kolmogorov and obtained his doctorate. He later became a professor there.

Volodymyr Olexandrovych Marchenko, the prominent Ukrainian mathematician known for his work in spectral theory and inverse scattering problems, studied and built his academic career in Kharkiv, Ukraine. Georg Forster (1754–1794) was a German naturalist, ethnologist, and writer who is known for accompanying James Cook on his second voyage around the world. He was not an oceanographer, nor did he receive an education at Harvard University (he was European and educated in Europe).
Dudley R. Herschbach, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, received his B.S. in Mathematics and M.S. in Chemistry from Stanford University before going on to earn his Ph.D. from Harvard University.

Carolyn R. Bertozzi did not attend Stanford University as a student. She earned her undergraduate degree from Harvard University (1988) and her Ph.D. from UC Berkeley (1993). She is, however, currently a professor at Stanford University, where she has been on the faculty since 2015.

Richard Smalley received his Ph.D. in chemistry from Princeton University in 1973, after completing his undergraduate studies at Hope College. So he did pursue part of his higher education at Princeton University.

Henry Taube received his B.S. and M.S. degrees from the University of Saskatchewan and his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley (1940). He did not pursue any part of his higher education at Princeton University or the University of Chicago. Peter Debije, known in English as Peter Debye, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1936 for his work on molecular structure, dipole moments, and the diffraction of X-rays and electrons in gases.

Mildred Dresselhaus, often called the 'Queen of Carbon Science,' received many prestigious honors including the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the Kavli Prize in Nanoscience, but she was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (or any Nobel Prize).

Gilbert Stork, the distinguished organic chemist known for his contributions to total synthesis of natural products, was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1982, recognizing his outstanding contributions to the field.

Harold Kroto was indeed a recipient of the Wolf Prize in Chemistry. He shared the 1993 Wolf Prize in Chemistry with Robert Curl and Richard Smalley for their discovery of fullerenes (buckminsterfullerene, C60), the same work for which they later received the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Niels Bohr was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922 for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them.

Hans Christian Ørsted (1777–1851) died before the Nobel Prize was established. The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901, so Ørsted could not have received one. He is best known for discovering the relationship between electricity and magnetism in 1820.
Martin Feldstein served as the Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Ronald Reagan from 1982 to 1984.

Gary Becker was a Nobel Prize-winning economist (1992) primarily known as an academic at the University of Chicago. He did not serve as Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers; he remained in academic roles throughout his career.

Richard Willstätter, the German chemist and Nobel Prize laureate (1915), did receive the Willard Gibbs Award, which is presented by the Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society to eminent chemists.

Walther Nernst, the German chemist known for the Nernst equation and the third law of thermodynamics, did receive the Willard Gibbs Award, which is presented by the Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society. He received it in 1929.

James Dewar, the Scottish chemist and physicist known for inventing the Dewar flask, was a Fellow of the Royal Society and received many honors, but he did not serve as President of the Royal Society.
