Sir Derek Barton was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1969, sharing it with Odd Hassel, for their contributions to the development of the concept of conformation and its application in chemistry.

Gabor A. Somorjai, the renowned surface chemist at UC Berkeley, has received many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (1998) and the National Medal of Science, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Saul Perlmutter was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011, sharing it with Brian P. Schmidt and Adam G. Riess for the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe through observations of distant supernovae.

Stephen Hawking was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Despite his groundbreaking theoretical work on black holes and cosmology, his theories were not experimentally confirmed during his lifetime, which is typically required for a Nobel Prize in Physics.

Gerhard Ertl studied at the Technical University of Munich (TU Munich), where he received his diploma in physics in 1961 and later his PhD in 1965, making TU Munich a key institution in his education.

Ahmed Zewail received his undergraduate and master's degrees from Alexandria University in Egypt, and his Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania. He then did postdoctoral work at UC Berkeley before joining Caltech. The Technical University of Munich was not part of his educational background.
Stuart A. Rice received his undergraduate degree from the City College of New York and his Ph.D. from Harvard University. He did not attend Yale University as a student.

George M. Whitesides received his undergraduate degree (A.B.) from Harvard University in 1960 and his Ph.D. from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in 1964. He did not attend Yale University.

Howard Walter Florey was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945, shared with Alexander Fleming and Ernst Boris Chain, for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases.

Frederick Sanger was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice (1958 and 1980), not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. His first prize was for determining the structure of insulin, and his second was for developing methods of DNA sequencing.
Adam Riess received his undergraduate degree from MIT and his PhD from Harvard University, so he was educated at both institutions mentioned.

Kip Stephen Thorne received his undergraduate degree from Caltech (California Institute of Technology) and his Ph.D. from Princeton University. He did not receive his education at Harvard University or MIT.

James Heckman is best known for receiving the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2000 (shared with Daniel McFadden). He is not known to have received the John Bates Clark Medal, which is awarded to American economists under 40.

Lars Peter Hansen is known for receiving the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2013 (shared with Eugene Fama and Robert Shiller), but he did not receive the John Bates Clark Medal, which is awarded to American economists under 40 deemed to have made the most significant contribution to economic thought.

Douglas Engelbart earned his BS from Oregon State University and then attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he received his MS and PhD in electrical engineering. He also received the Lemelson-MIT Prize in 1997 in recognition of his inventions, most notably the computer mouse and his pioneering work on interactive computing.

Fred Brooks did not attend the University of California, Berkeley. He received his undergraduate degree from Duke University and his PhD from Harvard University. Additionally, he is not known to have received the Lemelson-MIT Prize; his notable awards include the ACM Turing Award (1999), among others.

Klaus von Klitzing is best known for being awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1985 for discovering the quantum Hall effect. Karl Alexander Müller (K. Alex Müller) received many prestigious awards, most notably the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1987 (shared with J. Georg Bednorz) for discovering high-temperature superconductivity. He also received the ICTP Dirac Medal in 1994. Otto Hahn studied chemistry at the University of Marburg, where he also completed his doctorate in 1901 under the supervision of Theodor Zincke.

Ada Yonath received her undergraduate and graduate education in Israel — her bachelor's and master's degrees from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and her PhD from the Weizmann Institute of Science. Kip Stephen Thorne attended both institutions: he completed his undergraduate studies at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), earning his BS in 1962, and then went on to Princeton University, where he earned his PhD in 1965 under John Archibald Wheeler.
Carl Wieman did not attend Princeton University or Caltech. He received his B.S. from MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) and his Ph.D. from Stanford University.
Paul Dirac was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1933, which he shared with Erwin Schrödinger, for the discovery of new productive forms of atomic theory.

Stephen Hawking was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Despite his groundbreaking theoretical work on black holes and cosmology, his theories were not experimentally confirmed during his lifetime, which is generally required for the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Vitaly Lazarevich Ginzburg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2003, sharing it with Alexei Abrikosov and Anthony Leggett for their pioneering contributions to the theory of superconductors and superfluids.

Igor Vasilyevich Kurchatov, the Soviet nuclear physicist who led the USSR's atomic bomb project, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received numerous Soviet state honors, including Hero of Socialist Labour, but not the Nobel Prize.
Japetus Steenstrup (1813–1897) was a Danish naturalist who served as a professor at the University of Copenhagen, where he taught zoology and related subjects for many decades.

Peter Wilhelm Lund (1801–1880) was a Danish naturalist and paleontologist who spent most of his life conducting field research in Brazil, particularly at Lagoa Santa, Minas Gerais. He is renowned for his paleontological cave excavations rather than for holding a university teaching position.

Maurice Vincent Wilkes received both the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology (1992) and the IEEE John von Neumann Medal (1997), so the answer to whether he received at least one of these awards is yes.

Adi Shamir is renowned for his contributions to cryptography (RSA, secret sharing, etc.) and received the Turing Award in 2002, among other honors. However, based on my knowledge, he did not receive the IEEE John von Neumann Medal or the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology.

Rudolph A. Marcus was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1984/1985, recognizing his development of the Marcus theory of electron transfer reactions. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1992 for the same work.

Irving Langmuir, who died in 1957, could not have received the Wolf Prize in Chemistry because the Wolf Prize was not established until 1978. Langmuir was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1932, not the Wolf Prize.
Roger D. Kornberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2006 for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription.

Arthur Kornberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1959 (shared with Severo Ochoa), not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The prize recognized their discovery of the mechanisms of biological synthesis of RNA and DNA.
Claude Cohen-Tannoudji was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1997, sharing it with Steven Chu and William D. Phillips for their work on laser cooling and trapping of atoms.

Edward Witten has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He is renowned for his contributions to string theory and mathematical physics, and he received the Fields Medal in 1990 (a prestigious mathematics award), but he has not received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

James Chadwick was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935 for his discovery of the neutron, not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Gary Becker attended both institutions. He earned his undergraduate degree (B.A.) from Princeton University in 1951, and then went on to the University of Chicago, where he received his M.A. and Ph.D. and later spent much of his academic career.
Robert Solow did not attend Princeton University or the University of Chicago. He studied at Harvard University, where he received his undergraduate degree and his PhD in economics.

Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, the French physicist who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1997 for his work on laser cooling and trapping of atoms, was indeed awarded the CNRS Gold Medal (the highest scientific award in France) in 1996, shortly before receiving the Nobel Prize.

Georges Charpak was awarded the CNRS Gold Medal in 1981, recognizing his outstanding contributions to physics, particularly his work on particle detectors. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1992.

David Baltimore, the Nobel Prize-winning virologist, was awarded the National Medal of Science in 1999 by President Bill Clinton, recognizing his contributions to science including the discovery of reverse transcriptase.

Francis Crick, the British scientist who co-discovered the DNA double helix structure, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962 (shared with James Watson and Maurice Wilkins), but he was not awarded the U.S. National Medal of Science. David Baltimore was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1975, shared with Renato Dulbecco and Howard Temin, for their discoveries concerning the interaction between tumor viruses and the genetic material of the cell, specifically for the discovery of reverse transcriptase.

Roger Y. Tsien was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2008 (shared with Osamu Shimomura and Martin Chalfie) for the discovery and development of green fluorescent protein (GFP), not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

William Henry Bragg, along with his son William Lawrence Bragg, received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1915 for their work on the analysis of crystal structure by means of X-rays, which is a foundational area of crystallography.

Robert Robinson received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1947 (not Physics) for his work on plant products of biological importance, particularly alkaloids. He was an organic chemist and did not work in crystallography.

Adam Riess was awarded the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics in 2015, along with Saul Perlmutter and Brian Schmidt, for their discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe through observations of distant supernovae.

Joseph Hooton Taylor Jr. is best known for winning the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics (with Russell Hulse) for the discovery of a binary pulsar. Ernst Mayr satisfies all three conditions: he was a renowned ornithologist, he worked as a curator (at the American Museum of Natural History and later at the Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard), and he attended the University of Greifswald early in his academic career before transferring to the University of Berlin where he completed his PhD.

John Maynard Smith was a theoretical evolutionary biologist and geneticist. He trained as an engineer at Cambridge, later studied biology under J.B.S. K. C. Nicolaou, the renowned synthetic chemist known for his total synthesis of taxol and other complex molecules, has not received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. While he has received many other prestigious awards, the Nobel Prize is not among them.

Anthony Fauci has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While he is a highly respected immunologist and infectious disease expert who has received many honors, the Nobel Prize is not among them.

Ivan Matveevich Vinogradov (1891–1983), the prominent Soviet mathematician known for his work in analytic number theory, was educated at Saint Petersburg (Petrograd) University, not at Lomonosov Moscow State University. Douglas Engelbart earned his PhD in electrical engineering from the University of California, Berkeley in 1955, after completing his undergraduate studies at Oregon State University.

Ivan Sutherland received his bachelor's degree from Carnegie Institute of Technology (now Carnegie Mellon University), his master's degree from Caltech, and his Ph.D. from MIT in 1963. He did not attend the University of California, Berkeley.

Based on my knowledge of Robert Huber's awards and honors, I do not have reliable information indicating that he was awarded the Sir Hans Krebs Medal (given by FEBS). His well-documented major awards include the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1988), the Otto Warburg Medal, and others, but the Sir Hans Krebs Medal does not appear among his recognized honors in my knowledge.

Otto Hahn, the German chemist known for discovering nuclear fission and awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1944, was never awarded the Sir Hans Krebs Medal. The Sir Hans Krebs Medal is awarded by the Federation of European Biochemical Societies (FEBS) for contributions to biochemistry, a field unrelated to Hahn's work. Moreover, Hahn died in 1968, and the FEBS Hans Krebs Medal was established after Hans Krebs's death in 1981, making it impossible for Hahn to have received it.
Gerhard Ertl, a German physicist and chemist, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2007 for his studies of chemical processes on solid surfaces.

Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855) died before the Nobel Prize was established. The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901, nearly half a century after Gauss's death, so he could not have been a recipient.
Kenneth Arrow studied at Columbia University, where he earned his B.S. in Social Science in 1940 and later his Ph.D. in Economics in 1951.

Robert Solow studied at Harvard University, not Columbia University. He enrolled at Harvard in 1940, served in World War II, then returned to Harvard where he completed his undergraduate and doctoral degrees in economics (PhD under Wassily Leontief).

Kip Stephen Thorne was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017, sharing it with Rainer Weiss and Barry Barish for their contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.

Victor Frederick Weisskopf, despite being a highly distinguished theoretical physicist and making major contributions to quantum mechanics and nuclear physics, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received many other honors, including the National Medal of Science and the Wolf Prize, but the Nobel Prize was not among them.

Joseph E. Stiglitz served as the Chief Economist and Senior Vice President of the World Bank from 1997 to 2000, before his departure amid disagreements over IMF and World Bank policies during the global financial crisis of the late 1990s.

Oliver E. Williamson, the Nobel Prize-winning economist known for his work on transaction cost economics and the theory of the firm, spent his career primarily in academia (notably at UC Berkeley). He never served as Chief Economist of the World Bank; that position has been held by economists such as Joseph Stiglitz, Nicholas Stern, and Paul Romer, among others.
Steven Weinberg received his PhD from Princeton University in 1957, after completing his undergraduate studies at Cornell University and spending time at the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen.

Werner Heisenberg was a German physicist who studied at the University of Munich and the University of Göttingen in Germany. He did not attend Princeton University. He is associated with German academic institutions, not Princeton.

Carolyn R. Bertozzi received her undergraduate degree (B.A. in Chemistry) from Harvard University in 1988, and she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship (commonly known as the 'genius grant') in 1999, recognizing her pioneering work in chemistry and biology.

Herbert C. Brown (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1979) attended Wright Junior College and the University of Chicago, not Harvard University. He spent most of his academic career at Purdue University. Additionally, there is no record of him receiving a MacArthur Fellowship.

George Porter, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, studied at the University of Cambridge, where he completed his PhD under Ronald Norrish at Emmanuel College. He later held positions at Cambridge as well.

Peter Debye (Petrus Josephus Wilhelmus Debije) studied at the Technical University of Aachen (RWTH Aachen) and later at the University of Munich, where he obtained his PhD in 1908 under Arnold Sommerfeld. He did not study at the University of Cambridge.

John Charles Polanyi was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1986, sharing it with Dudley R. Herschbach and Yuan T. Lee for their contributions concerning the dynamics of chemical elementary processes.

Allen J. Bard, while a highly distinguished electrochemist who received many prestigious awards (such as the Wolf Prize in Chemistry and the National Medal of Science), was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Harry B. Gray, the renowned inorganic chemist at Caltech, received the Priestley Medal, which is the highest honor awarded by the American Chemical Society. He received it in 2004.

Peter G. Schultz is a highly accomplished chemist known for his work on expanding the genetic code and chemical biology, and has received numerous awards (including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry), but he is not known to have received the Priestley Medal, the American Chemical Society's highest honor.

Jean-Pierre Changeux did both: he studied at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris, and he received the Balzan Prize in 2001 for cognitive neurosciences. Since at least one (in fact both) of these conditions is true, the answer is yes.
Solomon H. Snyder did not attend the École Normale Supérieure, but he did receive the Balzan Prize (in 2003 for pharmacology). Since the question uses 'or,' the answer is yes.

Frank Macfarlane Burnet is best known for receiving the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1960 (shared with Peter Medawar) for his work on acquired immunological tolerance. He is not known to have received the Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research.

Frederick Gowland Hopkins did not receive the Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research. He is best known for receiving the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1929 for his discovery of vitamins. The Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research was established in 1945, and Hopkins (who died in 1947) was not among its recipients.
Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg (1795–1876) died in 1876, before the Leeuwenhoek Medal was first awarded in 1877. The inaugural recipient of the medal was Ferdinand Cohn, not Ehrenberg.

Alexander Agassiz, the marine zoologist and oceanographer, did not receive the Leeuwenhoek Medal. The Leeuwenhoek Medal is awarded by the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences for microbiology. Agassiz received other honors such as the Wollaston Medal from the Geological Society of London, but not the Leeuwenhoek Medal.
James D. Watson received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, shared with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, for their discovery of the molecular structure of DNA.

Paul Berg received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980 (shared with Walter Gilbert and Frederick Sanger) for his fundamental studies of the biochemistry of nucleic acids, particularly recombinant DNA. He did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Barry Marshall, along with Robin Warren, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005 for their discovery of the bacterium Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

Robert Gallo was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Despite his significant contributions to HIV/AIDS research, the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of HIV was awarded to Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier (along with Harald zur Hausen for separate work on HPV). Gallo's exclusion was considered controversial by many in the scientific community.

Joan Steitz earned her PhD from Harvard University, where she studied under James Watson. She completed her doctoral work there in the 1960s before going on to a distinguished career at Yale University.
Gertrude B. Elion attended Hunter College for her undergraduate degree and later did graduate work at New York University. She did not attend Harvard University.

Francis Crick studied at the University of Cambridge, where he earned his PhD and conducted the famous research with James Watson that led to the discovery of the double helix structure of DNA in 1953.

Selman Waksman did not study at the University of Cambridge. He received his B.S. and M.S. degrees from Rutgers College and earned his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley. He spent most of his academic career at Rutgers University.

Serge Haroche was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2012, sharing it with David J. Wineland, for ground-breaking experimental methods that enable measuring and manipulation of individual quantum systems.

Hubert Reeves, the Canadian-French astrophysicist, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. While he was highly respected for his work in nuclear astrophysics and science communication, he did not receive a Nobel Prize.

Shinya Yamanaka received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2012, shared with John B. Gurdon, for the discovery that mature cells can be reprogrammed to become pluripotent (induced pluripotent stem cells, iPSCs).

Anthony Fauci has not received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. While he has received many prestigious awards, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the Nobel Prize is not among them.

Yuan T. Lee, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned his Ph.D. and later served as a professor and researcher at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Elias James Corey attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned his B.S. and Ph.D. degrees. He spent most of his academic career at Harvard University. He was not associated with the University of California, Berkeley as a student.

Rudolf Mössbauer, the German physicist known for discovering the Mössbauer effect, was awarded the Elliott Cresson Medal by the Franklin Institute in 1961, the same year he received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Hans Bethe was awarded the Elliott Cresson Medal by the Franklin Institute, one of many prestigious honors he received throughout his distinguished career in physics.

Friedrich Engels co-owned and managed the textile firm Ermen & Engels in Manchester, England, which his family had interests in. He worked there as a businessman for many years, which provided him financial income (including support for Karl Marx) and firsthand experience of industrial capitalism. So while he is primarily known as a philosopher and political theorist, he did function as an entrepreneur/businessman.

Karl Marx was a philosopher, economist, political theorist, and revolutionary socialist, best known for writing 'The Communist Manifesto' and 'Das Kapital.' He was not an entrepreneur; in fact, he was a critic of capitalism and the bourgeois entrepreneurial class.
Pavel Alekseyevich Cherenkov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1958, shared with Ilya Frank and Igor Tamm, for the discovery and interpretation of the Cherenkov effect (Cherenkov radiation).

Georgy Flyorov (Flerov) was a prominent Soviet nuclear physicist known for his work on nuclear fission and the discovery of new elements (element 114, flerovium, is named after him), but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Carolyn R. Bertozzi was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2022, sharing it with Morten Meldal and K. Barry Sharpless for the development of click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry.

Stuart L. Schreiber, the prominent chemical biologist at Harvard University known for his work in chemical genetics and diversity-oriented synthesis, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as of my knowledge cutoff.

Elizabeth Blackburn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2009, which she shared with Carol Greider and Jack Szostak for their discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase.

Jean-Pierre Changeux is a renowned French neuroscientist known for his work on the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He has received other prestigious awards, but the Nobel Prize is not among them.

Ada Yonath received both the Israel Prize (2002) and the Harvey Prize (2002). She is an Israeli structural biologist renowned for her work on the ribosome, and she later won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009.

Roger Y. Tsien received the Harvey Prize, awarded by the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology. He received it in 2004, along with Martin Chalfie and Osamu Shimomura, for their work on green fluorescent protein (GFP). He did not receive the Israel Prize, which is a separate award given by the State of Israel typically to Israeli citizens.
Robert H. Grubbs received his Ph.D. in chemistry from Columbia University, where he studied under Ronald Breslow. So yes, he attended Columbia University as part of his graduate education.

Frances Arnold attended Princeton University for her undergraduate degree (B.S. in Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, 1979) and earned her Ph.D. in Chemical Engineering from the University of California, Berkeley in 1985. She did not attend Columbia University.

Ryōji Noyori, the Japanese chemist and Nobel laureate, was indeed awarded the Arthur C. Cope Award by the American Chemical Society in 1997, recognizing his outstanding contributions to organic chemistry, particularly his work on asymmetric catalysis.

Ahmed H. Zewail, the Egyptian-American chemist known for his work in femtochemistry and recipient of the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, does not appear to have been awarded the Arthur C. Cope Award. The Arthur C. Cope Award is given by the American Chemical Society for outstanding achievements in organic chemistry, which is not Zewail's primary field. He received numerous other honors, but the Arthur C. Cope Award is not among them.

Jonas Salk did spend time at the University of Michigan. After earning his M.D. from New York University School of Medicine in 1939, he went to the University of Michigan on a fellowship to work with Dr. Thomas Francis Jr. on influenza research, remaining there from around 1941 to 1947.

Renato Dulbecco studied medicine at the University of Turin in Italy, where he earned his MD. After emigrating to the United States, he worked at Indiana University (with Salvador Luria) and later at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). He is not known to have attended the University of Michigan.

Philippe Aghion received his PhD from MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), not Harvard University. He later became a professor at Harvard University, but his doctoral studies were conducted at MIT.

Thomas Piketty did not study at Harvard University. He completed his education in France at the École Normale Supérieure and received his PhD from the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales (EHESS), also in conjunction with the London School of Economics. Early in his career, he taught at MIT, but he was never a student at Harvard.

Melvin Calvin received his Ph.D. from the University of Minnesota in 1935, and subsequently conducted postdoctoral research at the University of Manchester under Michael Polanyi. So he pursued parts of his education at both institutions.

Rudolph A. Marcus received both his B.Sc. (1943) and Ph.D. (1946) from McGill University in Montreal, Canada. He did not pursue any part of his education at the University of Minnesota or the University of Manchester.
Richard Feynman attended both institutions: he completed his undergraduate degree at MIT and then went on to earn his Ph.D. from Princeton University.

Hans Bethe did not attend MIT or Princeton University. He studied at the University of Frankfurt and received his PhD from the University of Munich under Arnold Sommerfeld in 1928. He later became a professor at Cornell University, where he spent most of his American career.
Pavel Alekseyevich Cherenkov was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1958, shared with Ilya Frank and Igor Tamm, for the discovery and interpretation of the Cherenkov effect (Cherenkov radiation).

Mikhail Lavrentyev was a Soviet mathematician and scientist, founder of the Siberian Branch of the Soviet Academy of Sciences. He was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics; he received various Soviet state honors, but the Nobel Prize in Physics was never among them.

Sydney Brenner was awarded the Copley Medal by the Royal Society in 2005, in recognition of his distinguished contributions to biological sciences, particularly his work on the genetic code and model organisms like C. elegans.

Barbara McClintock, the Nobel Prize-winning geneticist known for discovering transposable elements, was not awarded the Copley Medal. Her major honors include the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, the National Medal of Science, and the Thomas Hunt Morgan Medal, among others, but the Copley Medal (awarded by the Royal Society of London) was not among them.

Joseph L. Goldstein, the Nobel Prize-winning biochemist, received his undergraduate (B.S.) degree from Washington and Lee University in Lexington, Virginia, graduating in 1962, before going on to earn his M.D. from the University of Texas Southwestern Medical School.
Stanley Cohen, the notable American biochemist and Nobel Prize laureate, was educated at Brooklyn College (B.A.) and the University of Michigan (Ph.D.), not at Washington and Lee University.

Victor Mikhailovich Glushkov was a prominent Soviet mathematician and cyberneticist who made significant contributions to the field of cybernetics, including foundational work in computer science, digital computers, and information theory in the USSR.

Nikolay Bogolyubov (1909–1992) was a prominent Soviet mathematician and theoretical physicist whose work focused on quantum field theory, statistical mechanics, dynamical systems, and mathematical physics (e.g., the Bogoliubov transformation, BBGKY hierarchy). He is not known for contributions to cybernetics, which was a separate field associated primarily with Norbert Wiener and, in the Soviet context, with figures like Anatoly Kitov and Viktor Glushkov.
Max Perutz was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1962, shared with John Kendrew, for their studies of the structures of globular proteins (hemoglobin and myoglobin).

Robert Wilhelm Bunsen (1811–1899) died before the Nobel Prize was established. The first Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded in 1901, two years after Bunsen's death, so he was never awarded the prize.

Trofim Lysenko is commonly described as a Soviet biologist (and agronomist). He directed the Institute of Genetics of the Soviet Academy of Sciences, working in biological and agricultural sciences, though he famously rejected Mendelian genetics and promoted his pseudoscientific 'Lysenkoism.'

The most prominent Alexander Vinogradov in science is Alexander Pavlovich Vinogradov (1895–1975), who was a Soviet geochemist and biogeochemist, not a biologist, geneticist, or botanist. He is known for his work in geochemistry and biogeochemistry, closely associated with Vladimir Vernadsky's school of thought.

Shinya Yamanaka received his M.D. from Kobe University School of Medicine in 1987, and he worked as a resident in orthopedic surgery before transitioning to a research career. Both conditions are true.

Rosalyn Yalow was an American medical physicist, not a surgeon. She earned her PhD in nuclear physics from the University of Illinois and spent her career at the Bronx Veterans Administration Hospital. She never worked as a surgeon nor attended Kobe University, which is a Japanese institution with no connection to her life or career.
Svante Arrhenius was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903 for his electrolytic theory of dissociation.

Allen J. Bard, while one of the most celebrated electrochemists and recipient of many prestigious awards (including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2008 and the National Medal of Science), was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Pierre-Gilles de Gennes was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1991 for discovering that methods developed for studying order phenomena in simple systems can be generalized to more complex forms of matter, particularly liquid crystals and polymers.

Richard Zare is a renowned chemist at Stanford University known for his work in laser chemistry and chemical dynamics. While he has received many prestigious awards, he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (or in any category, as of my knowledge cutoff).
Oliver E. Williamson was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2009, shared with Elinor Ostrom, for his analysis of economic governance, especially the boundaries of the firm.

William Baumol, despite being widely regarded as a highly deserving candidate for the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, never received the award. He passed away on May 4, 2017, and since the Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously, he was never recognized with this honor.

Sabir Yunusov was a prominent Soviet Uzbek chemist and academician renowned for his extensive work on alkaloid chemistry. He was indeed awarded the D. I. Mendeleyev Gold Medal in recognition of his outstanding contributions to chemistry, reflecting his significant impact on the field in the Soviet Union.

Alexander Pavlovich Vinogradov, the prominent Soviet geochemist and academician, was awarded the D. I. Mendeleev Gold Medal by the USSR Academy of Sciences in recognition of his outstanding contributions to geochemistry and related sciences.
Gérard Debreu received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1983 for his work on general equilibrium theory, incorporating new analytical methods into economic theory.

Edmond Malinvaud, the distinguished French economist known for his contributions to macroeconomics and econometrics, did not receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. While he was highly respected in the field and received other honors, the Nobel Prize was not among them.
Ronald Breslow received both his undergraduate degree (A.B.) and his doctoral degree (Ph.D.) from Harvard University, where he worked under the supervision of Nobel laureate R.B. Woodward.

Peter G. Schultz received his undergraduate and doctoral degrees from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), not Harvard University. He earned his B.S. and Ph.D. from Caltech before going on to positions at UC Berkeley and The Scripps Research Institute.
Selman Waksman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1952 for his discovery of streptomycin, the first antibiotic effective against tuberculosis.

Aaron Ciechanover was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2004, not in Physiology or Medicine. He shared the prize with Avram Hershko and Irwin Rose for the discovery of ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation.
C. A. R. Hoare (Tony Hoare) studied Classics and Philosophy (Greats) at Merton College, University of Oxford, and later returned to Oxford as a professor, where he spent much of his academic career.

Dana Scott (Dana Stewart Scott) pursued his undergraduate studies at UC Berkeley and completed his PhD at Princeton University in 1958 under Alonzo Church. While he later held a professorship at the University of Oxford (1972–1981), he did not pursue his studies there as a student.

Edward Witten was awarded the Fields Medal in 1990, making him one of the very few physicists to receive this prestigious mathematics award, recognized for his work connecting mathematics and string theory/quantum field theory.

Mildred Dresselhaus was a physicist and electrical engineer, not a mathematician. The Fields Medal is awarded to mathematicians under 40 years of age. Dresselhaus received many prestigious awards (e.g., National Medal of Science, Presidential Medal of Freedom, Kavli Prize), but not the Fields Medal.
Donald Knuth was awarded the National Medal of Science in 1979 by President Jimmy Carter, in addition to other honors such as the Turing Award (1974).

Juris Hartmanis, the computer scientist known for his foundational work in computational complexity theory, was awarded the National Medal of Science in 2013 by President Barack Obama, in addition to his earlier Turing Award (1993).
Harold Clayton Urey earned his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley in 1923, where he studied under the renowned chemist Gilbert N. Lewis.
Dorothy Hodgkin, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, studied at Somerville College, Oxford, and later did her PhD at Cambridge University. She did not attend the University of California, Berkeley.
Joseph E. Stiglitz served as Chief Economist and Senior Vice President of the World Bank from 1997 to 2000, before leaving amid disagreements over IMF and World Bank policies.

Robert Solow was an MIT economist and Nobel laureate known for his work on growth theory, but he never served as Chief Economist of the World Bank. That position has been held by economists such as Joseph Stiglitz, Nicholas Stern, and others, but not Solow.

Michael Sela, the Israeli immunologist, was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1998, together with Ruth Arnon, for their research on synthetic antigens and contributions to immunology, including the development of Copaxone for multiple sclerosis.
Özlem Türeci, co-founder of BioNTech, was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 2021, along with her husband Uğur Şahin and Drew Weissman, for their pioneering work on mRNA-based vaccines.
Charles Babbage held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge from 1828 to 1839, the same chair previously held by Isaac Newton and later by Stephen Hawking.

William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, held the Chair of Natural Philosophy at the University of Glasgow, not the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics. The Lucasian Chair is at the University of Cambridge and has been held by figures such as Isaac Newton, Charles Babbage, Paul Dirac, and Stephen Hawking.
Donald Knuth received the Turing Award in 1974, recognized for his major contributions to the analysis of algorithms and the design of programming languages.

Christos Papadimitriou, while a highly distinguished computer scientist known for his contributions to computational complexity theory, has not received the Turing Award. He has received other honors such as the Knuth Prize, but the Turing Award is not among them.

Jean Dausset was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1980, shared with Baruj Benacerraf and George Snell, for discoveries concerning genetically determined structures on the cell surface that regulate immunological reactions (HLA system).

Jean-Pierre Changeux is a renowned French neuroscientist known for his work on allosteric proteins and the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He has received other prestigious awards, such as the Balzan Prize, but the Nobel Prize is not among them.

Jane Goodall is renowned for her groundbreaking work as a primatologist and ethologist, most notably for her decades-long study of wild chimpanzees in Gombe Stream National Park, Tanzania, which fundamentally transformed our understanding of primate behavior.

Martin Rees, Baron Rees of Ludlow is a British cosmologist and astrophysicist, known for his work on galaxy formation, black holes, and cosmology. He has no known involvement in primatology or ethology.

Joseph L. Goldstein, along with Michael S. Brown, received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1985 for their discoveries concerning the regulation of cholesterol metabolism, particularly the LDL receptor.

Paul Berg received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980 (shared with Walter Gilbert and Frederick Sanger), not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He was recognized for his fundamental studies of the biochemistry of nucleic acids, particularly recombinant DNA.

Jean le Rond d'Alembert did both. He served as the perpetual secretary of the Académie française (the French Academy) from 1772 until his death in 1783. He also worked as a music theorist (musicologist), notably writing 'Éléments de musique théorique et pratique suivant les principes de M. Rameau' (1752), which helped popularize Rameau's theories of harmony.

Joseph Fourier served as the Permanent (Perpetual) Secretary of the Académie des Sciences (French Academy of Sciences) starting in 1822. He was not a musicologist; he was a mathematician and physicist famous for his work on heat transfer and Fourier series.

David Gross, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist, received his undergraduate degree from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and his Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley. He did not attend Harvard University.

Yoichiro Nambu did not attend Harvard University. He received his education at the University of Tokyo, where he earned his degrees. After coming to the United States, he was associated with the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton and then spent most of his career at the University of Chicago, where he became a distinguished professor.
Carl Wieman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2001, which he shared with Eric Cornell and Wolfgang Ketterle for the achievement of Bose-Einstein condensation in dilute gases of alkali atoms.

Peter Zoller, the Austrian theoretical physicist known for his work in quantum optics and quantum information, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He has received other prestigious honors, such as the Wolf Prize in Physics (2013, shared with Juan Ignacio Cirac) and the Dirac Medal, but not the Nobel Prize.
Chen Ning Yang was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957, shared with Tsung-Dao Lee, for their work on the violation of parity conservation in weak nuclear interactions.
Svante Arrhenius was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903, not Physics. He received it for his work on the electrolytic theory of dissociation.
Hermann Emil Fischer was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1902 for his work on sugar and purine syntheses.

Fritz Lipmann was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1953 (shared with Hans Krebs), not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He was recognized for his discovery of coenzyme A and its importance for intermediary metabolism.

Al-Biruni was a medieval Islamic polymath who worked across many disciplines. He wrote 'Kitab al-Saydana fi al-Tibb' (Book of Pharmacy and Materia Medica), a significant work on pharmacology and medicinal plants, which demonstrates that he worked in the areas of pharmacy and related botanical study, among many other fields.
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274) was a Persian polymath known primarily as a mathematician, astronomer, philosopher, and theologian. He was not a pharmacist or botanist.

Georgy Flyorov (1913–1990), the Soviet nuclear physicist known for co-discovering spontaneous fission of uranium and later leading the synthesis of new elements, studied at the Leningrad Polytechnic Institute, which is now known as Peter the Great Saint Petersburg State Polytechnical University.

Yuri Oganessian received his education at the Moscow Engineering Physics Institute (MEPhI), not at Peter the Great Saint Petersburg State Polytechnical University. He went on to work at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, where he became renowned for his research on superheavy elements.
Albert Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.

Arthur Stanley Eddington, despite his major contributions to astrophysics and his famous 1919 solar eclipse expedition confirming Einstein's general relativity, never received the Nobel Prize in Physics. He was awarded other honors such as the Royal Astronomical Society's Gold Medal and was knighted, but the Nobel Prize was not among his awards.
Selman Waksman received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1952 for his discovery of streptomycin, the first antibiotic effective against tuberculosis.

Emmanuelle Charpentier received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020, shared with Jennifer Doudna, for the development of CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology — not the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Evgeny Velikhov, the prominent Soviet and Russian physicist and vice president of the Soviet Academy of Sciences, was awarded the Order of Lenin, one of the highest honors in the Soviet Union, in recognition of his contributions to science and public service.

I do not have reliable information confirming that Igor Ternov (the Soviet physicist known for the Sokolov-Ternov effect) was specifically awarded the Order of Lenin. While he was a prominent Soviet scientist who received various honors, I cannot confirm this particular award.

Steven Weinberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1979, which he shared with Sheldon Glashow and Abdus Salam, for their contributions to the theory of the unified weak and electromagnetic interaction between elementary particles.

John Norris Bahcall was a renowned astrophysicist known for his work on solar neutrinos and the Hubble Space Telescope, but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. While his collaborator Raymond Davis Jr. received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2002 for detecting solar neutrinos, Bahcall was not included in that award.
James Heckman was awarded the John Bates Clark Medal in 1983, recognizing his contributions to economics. He later also received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2000.

George Akerlof was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2001 (shared with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz), but he was not awarded the John Bates Clark Medal, which is given to American economists under 40 who have made significant contributions to economic thought.
Svante Arrhenius was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903 for his theory of electrolytic dissociation.

Harry B. Gray, the prominent inorganic chemist at Caltech, has received many prestigious awards including the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, the National Medal of Science, and the Priestley Medal, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Francesco Brioschi (1824–1897), the Italian mathematician and founder of the Politecnico di Milano, served as a member of the Senate of the Kingdom of Italy (Senato del Regno), not the Chamber of Deputies. He was appointed as a life senator, which was the typical path for distinguished scientists and public figures of his era.
Enrico D'Ovidio, the Italian mathematician, served as a Senator of the Kingdom of Italy (appointed to the Senate in 1905), not as a member of the Chamber of Deputies.

Louis Agassiz was indeed a prominent geologist and glaciologist, best known for his pioneering work on glaciers and the ice age theory. He also attended the University of Zurich (among other institutions such as the Universities of Heidelberg and Munich) during his education. Both conditions in the question are satisfied.

David Attenborough studied natural sciences at Clare College, Cambridge, and worked as a broadcaster and natural historian for the BBC. He was not a geologist or glaciologist, nor did he attend the University of Zurich.
Karl Deisseroth received his undergraduate degree from Harvard University and later earned his M.D. and Ph.D. from Stanford University, where he also became a professor.

Joseph L. Goldstein completed his internship and residency at Massachusetts General Hospital, which is a primary teaching hospital affiliated with Harvard Medical School. While his formal degrees (B.S. from Washington and Lee University; M.D. from UT Southwestern Medical School) were not from Harvard or Stanford, his clinical training was conducted at a Harvard-affiliated institution.

César Milstein received numerous prestigious awards, including the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (1984), the Lasker Award, and the Gairdner Foundation International Award, but there is no evidence in my knowledge that he was awarded the Liebig Medal, which is typically associated with the German Chemical Society.
Avram Hershko was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2004, together with Aaron Ciechanover and Irwin Rose, for their discovery of ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation.

Allen J. Bard, the prominent electrochemist often called the 'father of modern electrochemistry,' did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Ben Shneiderman is a renowned computer scientist known for his contributions to human-computer interaction and information visualization, and has received many honors (such as the ACM CHI Lifetime Achievement Award). Stephen J. Benkovic, a distinguished chemist known for his work in bioorganic chemistry and enzyme mechanisms, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He has received other honors such as the National Medal of Science, but not the Nobel Prize.

Frederick Sanger received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, not in Physiology or Medicine. He was awarded it twice: in 1958 for determining the structure of insulin, and in 1980 for developing methods for DNA sequencing.

Francis Collins, the geneticist and former director of the NIH and the Human Genome Project, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He has received other honors, such as the Presidential Medal of Freedom, but not a Nobel Prize.
George Porter, the British chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1967, served as President of the Royal Society from 1985 to 1990.

Dorothy Hodgkin never served as President of the Royal Society. She was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1947 and received many honors, including the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964, but she did not hold the presidency of the Royal Society.

Charles Townes attended the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) for his doctoral education, earning his Ph.D. in physics in 1939. He had previously completed his undergraduate studies at Furman University and his master's degree at Duke University.

Ernest O. Lawrence did not attend the California Institute of Technology. He earned his undergraduate degree from the University of South Dakota, did graduate work at the University of Minnesota and University of Chicago, and received his PhD from Yale University in 1925. He later joined the faculty at the University of California, Berkeley, where he spent most of his career.

Richard Smalley earned his Ph.D. from Princeton University in 1973, where he studied chemistry under the supervision of Donald Levy and Lennard Wharton. He is best known for co-discovering fullerenes, for which he shared the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Herbert C. Brown, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, attended the University of Chicago, where he earned both his B.S. and Ph.D. degrees. He did not attend Princeton University. He spent the majority of his academic career as a professor at Purdue University.

Hermann Joseph Muller, the geneticist known for his work on X-ray induced mutations, was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1932, which supported his research and travel to Europe, including his time working in the Soviet Union.

Thomas Hunt Morgan, the Nobel Prize-winning geneticist known for his work on chromosomes and heredity, is not known to have been awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship. He received numerous other honors, most notably the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1933, but a Guggenheim Fellowship is not among the awards associated with him.

Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg held a medical degree and worked as a physician, in addition to his extensive work as a naturalist and microscopist. He also conducted significant early work in mycology (on fungi). Thus, at least one of the listed criteria (working as a physician or mycologist) applies to him.

Rodolfo Amando Philippi (Rudolf Amandus Philippi, 1808–1904) was trained as a physician and practiced medicine, in addition to being a prominent naturalist in Chile. He did work as a physician, satisfying that part of the condition.
Roger Y. Tsien pursued studies at both institutions. He completed his undergraduate studies at Harvard College and then went on to the University of Cambridge for his graduate work in physiology.
Robert H. Grubbs received his B.S. from the University of Florida and his Ph.D. from Columbia University. He did not pursue studies at Harvard College or the University of Cambridge.

Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov studied at Leningrad State University (now known as Saint Petersburg State University), where he graduated in 1933 and later became a prominent figure, eventually serving as its rector from 1952 to 1964.
Kolmogorov pursued his education at Moscow State University, where he enrolled in 1920, not at Saint Petersburg State University.
Harold Clayton Urey was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1934 for his discovery of deuterium (heavy hydrogen).

Steven Weinberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1979, not Chemistry. He shared it with Sheldon Glashow and Abdus Salam for their contributions to the theory of the unified weak and electromagnetic interaction between elementary particles.

Rudolf Mössbauer studied at the Technical University of Munich, where he earned his doctorate and later became a professor. He is closely associated with this institution throughout his academic career.

Anne L'Huillier received her education in France, studying at Pierre and Marie Curie University (Paris VI) where she earned her PhD. She did not attend the Technical University of Munich. She later became a professor at Lund University in Sweden.
Glenn T. Seaborg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1951, which he shared with Edwin McMillan, for their discoveries in the chemistry of the transuranium elements.

Susan Solomon, the renowned atmospheric scientist known for her research on the Antarctic ozone hole, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry related to ozone depletion was awarded to Paul Crutzen, Mario Molina, and F. Sherwood Rowland. Solomon has received other prestigious honors, such as the National Medal of Science and the Blue Planet Prize, but not the Nobel Prize.

Roderick MacKinnon was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003, sharing it with Peter Agre, for discoveries concerning channels in cell membranes, specifically his structural and mechanistic studies of ion channels.

James D. Watson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, shared with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, for their discovery of the molecular structure of DNA. It was not the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1957 for his work on nucleotides and nucleotide co-enzymes.

Joan Steitz, the prominent molecular biologist known for her pioneering work on RNA and snRNPs, has received many prestigious awards (such as the Lasker Award and Gairdner International Award), but she has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as of my knowledge cutoff.

John Hasbrouck van Vleck earned his Ph.D. from Harvard University in 1922, after completing his undergraduate degree at the University of Wisconsin in 1920. He later also spent much of his academic career as a professor at Harvard.

Ernest Orlando Lawrence received his bachelor's degree from the University of South Dakota, his master's degree from the University of Minnesota, and his PhD from Yale University. Harvard University was not part of his educational path.
Andrei Sakharov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975 for his efforts on behalf of human rights, disarmament, and international cooperation.

Nikolay Bogolyubov was a renowned Soviet mathematician and theoretical physicist known for his work in quantum field theory and statistical mechanics. He received various Soviet state prizes and scientific honors, but he was never awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
John McCarthy, the computer scientist who coined the term 'artificial intelligence,' was awarded the Turing Award in 1971 for his contributions to AI research.

Daphne Koller, while a highly accomplished computer scientist known for her work in probabilistic graphical models and machine learning (and co-founder of Coursera), has not been awarded the Turing Award. She has received other honors such as the MacArthur Fellowship, but the Turing Award is not among them.

Oliver Smithies was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 2002, shared with Mario Capecchi, for their development of gene targeting technology in mice. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2007.

Marshall Warren Nirenberg is best known for receiving the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1968 for deciphering the genetic code. There is no strong evidence in my knowledge that he was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine, which is a separate Israeli award given by the Wolf Foundation.
Samuel J. Danishefsky received his Ph.D. from Harvard University, where he worked under the supervision of E.J. Corey in organic chemistry.

Harry B. Gray received his B.S. from Western Kentucky University (1957) and his Ph.D. from Northwestern University (1960). He then did postdoctoral research at the University of Copenhagen. He did not receive any of his education at Harvard University.

Drew Weissman, along with Katalin Karikó, received the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences (in 2021) for their foundational work on mRNA modification technology, which was critical to the development of COVID-19 vaccines.

César Milstein, the Argentine biochemist known for his work on monoclonal antibodies, received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1984. He died in 2002, before the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences was established in 2013, so he could not have received it.

Sydney Brenner attended the University of Oxford, where he earned his DPhil. He initially studied at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa before moving to Oxford for his doctoral research.
Barry Marshall, the Australian physician and Nobel Prize laureate, attended the University of Western Australia, where he obtained his medical degree. He did not attend the University of Oxford.

Leo Esaki, the Japanese physicist who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1973 for his discovery of electron tunneling (the Esaki diode), worked at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center and was designated as an IBM Fellow, one of IBM's highest honors for distinguished scientists and engineers.

Hideki Yukawa was a Japanese theoretical physicist and Nobel Prize laureate (1949) known for predicting the existence of mesons. He was an academic researcher affiliated with Japanese universities, not an IBM employee. The IBM Fellow designation is awarded to IBM employees who have made outstanding contributions, so Yukawa would not have been eligible for or received this designation.

Richard Zare was awarded the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2005, sharing the prize with George M. Whitesides, in recognition of his pioneering contributions to the understanding of chemical reaction dynamics and laser chemistry.
Roger Adams, the prominent American organic chemist, died in 1971. The Wolf Prize in Chemistry was first awarded in 1978, several years after his death, so he could not have received it.
Werner Heisenberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1932 for the creation of quantum mechanics, specifically for the development of matrix mechanics and the uncertainty principle.

John Archibald Wheeler, despite being a highly influential theoretical physicist known for coining the term 'black hole' and his work on general relativity and nuclear physics, never received the Nobel Prize in Physics. He did receive other prestigious awards, such as the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1997.
Charles Stark Draper received his doctorate from MIT and spent his entire academic career there as a professor, eventually founding the Instrumentation Laboratory (now Draper Laboratory) at MIT.

Robert E. Kahn received his B.E.E. from the City College of New York and his M.A. and Ph.D. from Princeton University. While he later worked at MIT as a faculty member, he did not study there as a student.
Roger Y. Tsien was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2008, shared with Osamu Shimomura and Martin Chalfie, for the discovery and development of green fluorescent protein (GFP).

Christian de Duve was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1974 (shared with Albert Claude and George E. Palade) for discoveries concerning the structural and functional organization of the cell. He did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Stephen Hawking attended both the University of Oxford (for his undergraduate degree) and the University of Cambridge (for his PhD and where he spent most of his academic career).

Alan Guth, the American theoretical physicist known for developing inflationary cosmology, attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) for both his undergraduate and graduate education. He did not attend the University of Oxford or the University of Cambridge.
Stanley B. Prusiner was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1997 for his discovery of prions, a new biological principle of infection.

Thomas Cech was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1989 (shared with Sidney Altman) for his discovery of the catalytic properties of RNA. He did not receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Vitaly Lazarevich Ginzburg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2003, sharing it with Alexei Abrikosov and Anthony Leggett for their pioneering contributions to the theory of superconductors and superfluids.
Isaak Khalatnikov was a prominent Soviet/Russian theoretical physicist known for his work on superfluidity and cosmology (BKL singularity), but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Harold Clayton Urey was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1934 for his discovery of deuterium (heavy hydrogen).

Kyriacos Costa Nicolaou, while a highly acclaimed synthetic chemist known for landmark total syntheses such as taxol and brefeldin A, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He has received numerous other prestigious awards, but the Nobel Prize is not among them.
Arthur Compton was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1927 for his discovery of the Compton effect, which demonstrated the particle nature of electromagnetic radiation.

Rudolf Peierls, despite being a highly distinguished physicist known for contributions to quantum mechanics, solid-state physics, and the Frisch-Peierls memorandum, was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He received other honors, including a knighthood, but the Nobel Prize was not among his awards.
Milton Friedman attended both institutions. He earned his Master's degree from the University of Chicago and his PhD from Columbia University, so both were part of his educational background.

Paul Krugman did not attend Columbia University or the University of Chicago for his education. He received his undergraduate degree from Yale University and his PhD from MIT. He later held a professorship at Columbia University, but that was as faculty, not as a student.
Enrico Fermi enrolled at the University of Pisa in 1918 and earned his doctorate there in 1922. He also attended the Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa concurrently.
Werner Heisenberg studied at the University of Munich under Arnold Sommerfeld and later at the University of Göttingen under Max Born. He had no academic affiliation with the University of Pisa.

Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt) was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1904 for his investigations of the densities of the most important gases and for his discovery of argon in connection with these studies.

Arthur Stanley Eddington was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Despite his significant contributions to astrophysics, including confirming Einstein's general relativity during the 1919 solar eclipse and his work on stellar structure, he did not receive a Nobel Prize. He was, however, knighted and received other honors such as the Order of Merit.

Paul Langevin spent time studying at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge under J.J. Thomson around 1897-1898, as part of his scientific education before returning to France to complete his doctorate.

François Arago was a French scientist who received his education in France, most notably at the École Polytechnique in Paris. He had no educational connection to the University of Cambridge in England.
Yuan T. Lee was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1986, sharing it with Dudley R. Herschbach and John C. Polanyi for their contributions to the dynamics of chemical elementary processes.

Frank Albert Cotton was a highly acclaimed American inorganic chemist known for his work on metal-metal bonds and cotton's contributions to organometallic chemistry, but he was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, despite being considered a strong candidate multiple times during his career.

Kip Stephen Thorne was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017, jointly with Rainer Weiss and Barry Barish, for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.

John Archibald Wheeler, despite his enormous contributions to theoretical physics (including popularizing the term 'black hole' and work on general relativity and nuclear fission), was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. He did receive other honors, such as the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1997.

Isabella Karle was an American chemist who specialized in X-ray crystallography. She worked at the Naval Research Laboratory and made significant contributions to the field, including developing methods for determining molecular structures using X-ray diffraction.

Allen J. Bard was an American chemist known for his work in electrochemistry, not crystallography. He is often called the 'father of modern electrochemistry' and made major contributions to electroanalytical chemistry, photoelectrochemistry, and scanning electrochemical microscopy.

Murray Gell-Mann was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1969 for his contributions and discoveries concerning the classification of elementary particles and their interactions, particularly his work on quarks and the eightfold way.

Alan Guth, the physicist who proposed the theory of cosmic inflation, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics as of my knowledge cutoff. While he has received numerous prestigious awards such as the Kavli Prize in Astrophysics and the Gruber Cosmology Prize, the Nobel Prize in Physics has not been among them.

Kip Stephen Thorne was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017, sharing it with Rainer Weiss and Barry Barish for their contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.

Vera Rubin, the astronomer famous for her work on galaxy rotation curves and dark matter evidence, never received the Nobel Prize in Physics. She was widely considered deserving of the prize but passed away in December 2016 without having been awarded it.
Pierre-Gilles de Gennes was awarded the Lorentz Medal in 1990 by the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences, shortly before he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1991.

Peter Higgs was awarded the Matteucci Medal (by the Italian National Academy of Sciences), among his many honors that also include the Nobel Prize in Physics (2013) and the Wolf Prize in Physics (2004).
Gordon Plotkin completed his PhD at the University of Edinburgh, and he has also spent much of his academic career there as a professor. So yes, he studied at the University of Edinburgh.
Bjarne Stroustrup studied at Aarhus University in Denmark for his undergraduate degree and then completed his PhD at the University of Cambridge in England, not the University of Edinburgh.

Jerry A. Hausman, the prominent MIT econometrician known for the Hausman specification test, has received various honors in economics, but he was not awarded the John Bates Clark Medal. The Clark Medal is given to an American economist under 40 who has made significant contributions, and Hausman is not among its recipients.

Leonid Hurwicz, while a highly distinguished economist who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2007, was not awarded the John Bates Clark Medal. The Clark Medal is given to an American economist under the age of 40, and Hurwicz did not receive this particular award during his career.
Glenn T. Seaborg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1951, which he shared with Edwin McMillan, for their discoveries in the chemistry of the transuranium elements.

Francis Collins, the geneticist known for leading the Human Genome Project and serving as director of the NIH, has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He has received other honors, such as the Presidential Medal of Freedom, but not a Nobel Prize.
William Ramsay was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1904 for his discovery of the noble gases (argon, neon, krypton, and xenon) and their places in the periodic table.

Sir Alan Battersby, the renowned British organic chemist known for his work on biosynthesis of natural products, did not receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Although he was highly decorated—winning awards such as the Wolf Prize in Chemistry (2000) and the Copley Medal—the Nobel Prize was not among his honors.

Alexander Fleming was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945, along with Ernst Boris Chain and Howard Florey, for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases.

Salvador Moncada was not awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Despite his significant contributions to the discovery of nitric oxide's role as a signaling molecule (including work on prostacyclin and nitric oxide), the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for nitric oxide research was awarded to Robert F. Furchgott, Louis J. Ignarro, and Ferid Murad. Moncada's exclusion was considered controversial by many in the scientific community.

Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff did pursue education at Leiden University. He studied there as part of his academic training before moving on to study under Kekulé in Bonn and later working in Paris in Adolphe Wurtz's laboratory. He ultimately received his doctorate from Utrecht University in 1874.
Richard Willstätter pursued his education at the University of Munich, where he studied under Adolf von Baeyer. He did not study at Leiden University or the University of Paris.

Peter Simon Pallas (1741–1811) was trained in medicine and received a medical degree, but he is not known to have practiced as a physician. His career was devoted to natural history, zoology, and botany, most famously through his extensive explorations and scientific work in Russia under Catherine the Great.

Georg Forster (1754–1794) was a German naturalist, ethnologist, travel writer, and political activist. He is best known for accompanying his father on Captain Cook's second voyage and for his scientific and literary work. He was not a physician and did not practice medicine; he worked as a naturalist, academic, and librarian.

César Milstein was awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1980, shared with Leo Sachs and James L. Gowans, for his work on immunology and the development of monoclonal antibodies. He later also received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1984.

Howard Walter Florey was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945 (shared with Alexander Fleming and Ernst Boris Chain) for his work on penicillin. However, he was not awarded the Wolf Prize in Medicine. Additionally, Florey died in 1968, and the Wolf Prize was not established until 1978, making it impossible for him to have received it.
Manfred Eigen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1967, sharing it with Ronald George Wreyford Norrish and George Porter for their work on extremely fast chemical reactions.
Elliott H. Lieb is a renowned mathematical physicist who was awarded the Abel Prize in 2022, but he has not been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Pierre-Gilles de Gennes was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1991 for discovering that methods developed for studying order phenomena in simple systems can be generalized to more complex forms of matter, particularly liquid crystals and polymers.
Walter Kohn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1998, not Physics. He received it for his development of density-functional theory.

Linus Pauling was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. He is one of the very few individuals to have won two Nobel Prizes, the other being the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954.
F. Sherwood Rowland was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995 (shared with Mario Molina and Paul Crutzen) for his work on the depletion of the ozone layer, not the Nobel Peace Prize.
William Lawrence Bragg was awarded the Copley Medal by the Royal Society in 1966, recognizing his outstanding contributions to the study of X-ray crystallography and his development of Bragg's law.
Arthur Compton, known for discovering the Compton effect, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1927, but he was not awarded the Copley Medal, which is given by the Royal Society of London.
Richard Dawkins studied at the University of Oxford, where he earned his Bachelor's degree and D.Phil. (doctorate) in zoology, working under Nobel Prize-winning ethologist Nikolaas Tinbergen.
Ernst Mayr received his education in Germany, earning his PhD from the University of Berlin in 1926. He did not study at the University of Oxford.
Roger Y. Tsien attended the University of Cambridge for his graduate studies, where he earned his PhD from Churchill College, before going on to his distinguished career in biochemistry.

Stanley B. Prusiner attended the University of Pennsylvania for his undergraduate studies and received his MD from the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine. He did not attend the University of Cambridge.

Peter Debije, known in English as Peter Debye, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1936 for his contributions to knowledge of molecular structure through his investigations on dipole moments and the diffraction of X-rays and electrons in gases.
Peter Grünberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2007, not Chemistry. He shared the prize with Albert Fert for their independent discovery of giant magnetoresistance (GMR).
